title: Chicago Bears Artwork: Remembering Stu & Lew Merrell
summary: Back in 2021, I published a story on the history of Chicago Bears artwork centered on an artist named Jerry Keefe. The late cartoonist drew his last program cover in 1961 for the Chicago Bears, but the images kept showing up in new ways, and I wanted to tell a story that seemed to be […]
full_text: Back in 2021, I published a story on the history of Chicago Bears artwork centered on an artist named Jerry Keefe. The late cartoonist drew his last program cover in 1961 for the Chicago Bears, but the images kept showing up in new ways, and I wanted to tell a story that seemed to be making its way back into relevance with the Bears working with local artists for gameday program cover images. When I published the story, I had collected a few of the Keefe programs. I eventually framed some of my favorites and hung them on the wall behind my desk, making for a killer background for the YouTube livestreams for Bear & Balanced. The problem is, I just kept collecting, eventually nabbing a copy of each of the programs with a Keefe cover. That led to interactions with fellow collectors who “might be willing to part with this rare program” if I’d be interested. So, the collection expanded to include a 1939 with a Stu Merrell cover. This is where I discovered my mistake. In the article, I said that Stu “Merrell drew the cover art while his dad, Lew Merrell, edited programs for the Bears.” Not exactly. Stu Merrell, a former Northwestern University baseball captain, was the impetus for the Bears to develop a more professional looking program. He drew all the 1939 covers and inside the programs, featured cartoon images of Bears players with little “fun fact” nuggets. Below shows the 1939 cover against that team up north with Joe Maniaci next to an insert “comic” featuring then rookie QB Sid Luckman. Stu died a tragic death on September 16, 1940. Heading to the offices managed by his father to work on the Bears programs for the upcoming 1940 season, Stu walked into the elevator with no car present and fell 16 feet, sustaining injuries that would claim his life. In the home opener against the Detroit Lions, the Bears featured the following story on the death of Stuart Merrell, giving him credit for upping the level of game programs. Stu would be given credit as editor of the 1940 programs. Presumedly, Lew helped finalize the programs and eventually took over as editor in 1941. It was Lew that guided the programs from 1941-1962. Lew was an accomplished cartoonist and owner of a commercial cartoon service called Merrell Features. While he never drew a program cover, he did continue on with player cartoons that would serve as delightful surprises when flipping through programs. Combined, Stu and Lew drew dozens of cartoons over a 23-year period, most appearing in the 1940s. Some cartoons would be reused, likely helping fill out program pages when needed. Lew included cartoons of opponents in 1943. In 1949, they featured photos instead of drawings as the central image. There were a couple of instances of Lew featuring a player originally drawn by Stu (Joe Stydahar and Danny Fortmann below) but for the most part, the two covered all the major and most of the minor players from the dynastic Bears. Some of the images were clearly commissioned by a company, like a series from a local candy company running a full-page ad with a drawing of a member of the coaching staff. Ray Bray, a good Bears player and entrepreneur, must have liked his cartoon so much that it became an ad buy for Ray Bray’s Cadillac (pictured below). By 1962, Lew was well into his 70s, and while the cartoons had largely stopped near the end of the run, it looked like he was ready to create one last series of legends, but only publishing the gem below on Bronko Nagurski in one of his final programs. Below are the known cartoons and inserts drawn by Stu and Lew Merrell. A note on organizations: After the 1939 covers, I started with Hall of Fame players, many of whom have multiple drawings. After Ed Sprinkle, I prioritized those that had different drawings throughout the years followed by players with single entries. I ended with the lesser-known players from the Bears’ “Hall of Fame” series (old-timers at the time who likely had some business in the area), the coaches, and finally the opponent series. I think they serve as a fascinating timepiece of a bygone era. Let me know in the comments which one is your favorite.

full_text: Photo courtesy of USAA Yesterday at Halas Hall, the Chicago Bears and USAA held their annual Salute to Service NFL Boot Camp , where service members based at Naval Station Great Lakes (IL) got to compete in drills similar to those used by NFL coaches to evaluate players. Those drills included the 40-yard dash, broad jump, three-cone shuttle, receiving gauntlet, and the quarterback arm challenge. They also got to participate in a fast-paced viral reaction challenge, testing their reflexes as they tried to catch falling batons as quickly as possible. After an introduction from Bears’ legend Lance Briggs and Bears’ Assistant General Manager Jeff King, the service members were split into teams to compete, with the winning team receiving tickets to this year’s Bears’ Salute to Service Game presented by USAA. The invited military members got to hang out with Briggs as he coached them through the drills, and they also got to stick around and watch what turned out to be a very demanding practice from a VIP viewing location. “ USAA’s Salute to Service NFL Boot Camp ” represents the evolution of authentic military appreciation events that USAA and the Bears have created to foster an understanding and appreciation for the local military community, bringing our military closer to a game they love. USAA is the Official Salute to Service Partner of the Chicago Bears, and you can find more info about USAA here: usaa.com The #Bears hosted their annual "USAA’s Salute to Service NFL Boot Camp" today at Halas Hall with 100 military members from Naval Station Great Lakes, participating in NFL drills with Bears legend Lance Briggs. 📹 courtesy of @USAA pic.twitter.com/UAG0gr8CNp — Lester A. title: Chicago Bears Question of the Day: Will injuries in the secondary derail the season?
summary: I’ve been trying to argue on behalf of the Chicago Bears’ secondary for three seasons now. There is just too much talent to ignore. This year, Jaylon Johnson, Kyler Gordon, Coby Bryant, Dillon Thieneman, Tyrique Stevenson, Malik Muhammad, Terrell Smith, and Cam Lewis are a formidable group. Throw in the likes of past Bears Kevin […]
full_text: Jun 5, 2024; Lake Forest, IL, USA; Chicago Bears cornerback Kyler Gordon (6) looks on during the team's minicamp at Halas Hall. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con I’ve been trying to argue on behalf of the Chicago Bears’ secondary for three seasons now. There is just too much talent to ignore. This year, Jaylon Johnson, Kyler Gordon, Coby Bryant, Dillon Thieneman, Tyrique Stevenson, Malik Muhammad, Terrell Smith, and Cam Lewis are a formidable group. Throw in the likes of past Bears Kevin Byard, Jaquan Brisker, Nashon Wright, and more and the Bears have been swarming in talent over the last few years. Despite leading the league in takeaways last season, it still felt like the secondary over the last few seasons has been underperforming. A lot of that is due to persisting injuries to important talents. The 2026 offseason has not been kind to this unit so far, either. As it stands, the Bears have already had injuries to the following players at safety, cornerback, and nickelback: CB Kyler Gordon remains on the PUP list with a calf injury. S Coby Bryant is out 4-6 months. CB Terrell Smith is hurt again. DB Cam Lewis has been dealing with an ankle injury. CB Jaylon Jones has missed some time with an undisclosed injury. DB Dallis Flowers is on the IR and may have an injury settlement. Meanwhile, the Bears’ top two outside cornerbacks, Tyrique Stevens and Jaylon Johnson, have dealt with injuries of their own in the past couple of seasons. All of this is to say, the 2026 Bears secondary looks great on paper, but paper doesn’t play. So on a defense that already has question marks up front, it’s fair to wonder if these injuries could derail an otherwise promising season. Will injuries in the Bears’ secondary derail the season? I don’t think it is going to help the Bears to have nagging injuries in the secondary (obviously) but I also don’t think it will derail their season. Here’s why. Last season, the Bears found themselves with a variety of injuries in the secondary, with a few being significant. Kyler Gordon missed 14 games Jaylon Johnson missed 10 games (and didn’t look like himself when he did play) Nick McCloud missed 3 games Jaquan Brisker had nagging injuries all season. Tyrique Stevenson missed 3 games. Josh Blackwell missed 2 games. Terrell Smith missed the entire season. The Bears had issues with injuries in the secondary last season, and they figured out how to scheme around it. They found players to plug in with CJ Gardner-Johnson and Nashon Wright. They cobbled together starts from Nick Mcleod and Jaylon Jones in the slot. Even with all of the turbulence, they managed a league-leading 23 INTs, an indication of good coaching and good positioning. Still, you can’t have schmucks out there playing a ton of downs – you require talented players to make game changing plays. Enter several new starting and depth level pieces: Drafting Dillon Thieneman and Malik Muhammad Signed Coby Bryant (who has not had major injury issues previously) Signed a major depth piece in Xavier Woods. Signed several other depth pieces in Marlen Sewell, William Wright, Beanie Bishop Jr., and Brandon Hill (who was just waived). In the last year, Ryan Poles’ roster management has switched from trying to find feature talent to building up the depth, and that is the sign of a team preparing for a deep playoff run. If Kyler has to miss a few games, you’ve got Malik Muhammad, Josh Blackwell, Jaylon Jones, and Cam Lewis that can rotate in. An injury to JJ or Tyrique? Malik, Dontae Manning, Terrell Smith, and Beanie Bishop are available. Coby’s knee gets reaggravated? Xavier Woods, Elijah Hicks, and Cam Lewis are capable of stepping up. The Bears have legitimate depth that can sustain injuries. Now, there is a limit — and the Bears are testing it right now with the number of players getting hampered throughout camp. However, Dennis Allen, Ben Johnson, and Ryan Poles are building a track record proving their ability to plug the holes and keep things moving. Now it’s your turn! Will injuries to the Bears’ secondary derail their season? Sound off in the comments!

title: Bengals’ value rises but still listed as least valuable NFL franchise
summary: It is no secret that the Cincinnati Bengals have been called a “cheap” NFL franchise over the years. We have seen big changes in how they operate over the last half-decade, and with NFL television revenue, they’re always going to turn a profit. It is basically impossible not to. While they will make plenty of […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - MAY 12: Cincinnati Bengals owner Mike Brown looks on during a rookie camp at Paul Brown Stadium on May 12, 2013 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Joe Robbins/Getty Images) | Getty Images It is no secret that the Cincinnati Bengals have been called a “cheap” NFL franchise over the years. We have seen big changes in how they operate over the last half-decade, and with NFL television revenue, they’re always going to turn a profit. It is basically impossible not to. While they will make plenty of money each season, Sportico released rankings of the most valuable NFL franchises , and Cincinnati was ranked dead last. For reference, they were valued at $7.4 billion, which is only small in this regard, though it is a 35% increase from last year. “The Cincinnati Bengals have been parked at No. 32 for seven straight years in Sportico ’s annual NFL team valuations. The small-market club plays in an older stadium, ranks near the bottom on local revenue and lacks a national brand from its Super Bowl trophy-less history.“ That shouldn’t come as much of a surprise to anyone. Cincinnati doesn’t have the mega stadium, the “Patriot Place” style complex outside of their stadium, or an owner with billions of dollars from other ventures. They are, to this day, a family-run organization passed down from one of the founding fathers of football. And even with the Bengals’ 32nd-ranked valuation, they are still one of the most valuable sports franchises in the world, as the article explains. “Yet there are only six sports franchises on the planet outside the NFL that are worth more than the Bengals. The list includes three from the NBA, two in MLB and LaLiga’s Real Madrid. The NFL’s least valuable team is worth $7.4 billion, by Sportico ’s count, and all 32 teams land among the world’s 40 most valuable “ sports franchises .” The Brown family is still making plenty of money, including a $453 million check sent to them by the NFL for TV revenue. Will they ever match the value of the Dallas Cowboys? Probably not. In reality, they don’t need to.

title: 3 key roster battles to watch in Bengals vs. Lions
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals will host their preseason opener Thursday when they face the Detroit Lions. With that in mind, here are three important position battles to watch for as the night unfolds. Nickel Corner Jalen Davis is the likely starter at the position to begin the season after a strong finish to the season last […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals tight end Tanner Hudson (87) catches a pass during the Cincinnati Bengals practice in Cincinnati on Tuesday, May 27, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Cincinnati Bengals will host their preseason opener Thursday when they face the Detroit Lions. With that in mind, here are three important position battles to watch for as the night unfolds. Nickel Corner Jalen Davis is the likely starter at the position to begin the season after a strong finish to the season last year. His primary backup at the position seems a bit more up for grabs. Ja’Sir Taylor was a veteran addition the Bengals brought in this offseason. Taylor has 65 games of NFL experience, which could help him make the 53-man roster. The player that can push him for that spot on the roster is Bralyn Lux. Lux was getting some run with the first-team defense recently when Davis was given a rest day. While Lux spent most of his rookie season on the practice squad, the Bengals did call him up to the active roster for the final three games of the season last year. Lux is a player I will be watching closely on Thursday. Bralyn Lux pic.twitter.com/4X9n0lJXBS — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 9, 2025 Tight End Mike Gesicki and Drew Sample are roster locks coming into the season. Erick All Jr. will not play during the preseason game on Thursday, but the Bengals love the versatility they get from him when he is healthy. The injury history makes the rest of what they do at this position more interesting. Tanner Hudson has made plays when his number is called, and has been a staple on special teams the past couple of seasons. As of right now, he is likely to be the fourth tight end on the roster, if they choose to keep only four this year. The Bengals also drafted Jack Endries in the seventh round of the 2026 draft. It has been a quiet camp for Endries, but the talented pass catcher could make a push starting Thursday. The Bengals could even choose to keep five tight ends, but with the depth elsewhere this year, I have a tough time seeing that. This roster battle will likely come down to the veteran Hudson and the rookie Endries for the final spot on the 53-man roster. Endries will have to go out and earn it starting on Thursday. Offensive Tackle If the Bengals choose to keep 10 offensive linemen, there will be a battle for that 10th and final spot. Cody Ford is set to be the primary backup at the tackle position, but they could decide to keep another player on the 53-man roster at that position. Candidates for that spot include Andrew Coker and Javon Foster. Both players were on the Bengals practice squad last season. The Bengals also added undrafted free agents Christian Jones and Corey Robinson II this year. Robinson is currently listed on the Bengals roster as a guard, but he played tackle in college. Andrew Coker vs. Indianapolis Colts pic.twitter.com/E65YhKWTob — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 24, 2025 One of those players will have to impress for the Bengals to opt to keep 10 offensive linemen. If not, I can see the Bengals keeping just nine players at the spot to start the season. Guys like Brian Parker II and Jalen Rivers could also kick out to tackle in a pinch, which may be a reason they go light at the position. How the depth of the position plays out is certainly something to watch on Thursday. What roster battles are you most excited to watch this week?

title: Bengals News: Zac Taylor has been breaking an NFL rule all this time
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals play football against someone other than themselves this week! That’s not the only thing going on though. We’re nearing preseason Week 1, which means the regular season is also just around the corner. There is plenty going on, though. The front office will begin the process of deciding who will make the […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor walks the field during Bengals practice at the Kettering Practice Fields in Cincinnati, Ohio, on Thursday, August 6, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Cincinnati Bengals play football against someone other than themselves this week! That’s not the only thing going on though. We’re nearing preseason Week 1, which means the regular season is also just around the corner. There is plenty going on, though. The front office will begin the process of deciding who will make the final 53-man roster once they get some game tape on the second and third string guys, and a lot more as the greatest professional sports league in the world comes back to us. Here are some other goings on as we approach the 24-hour mark until the Bengals’ preseason opener: Starting this season, the NFL will allow someone other than the head coach to throw a challenge flag. The only issue with that, is the Bengals have been doing it illegally for the last several seasons . “We’ve been breaking the rule for eight years,” Taylor joked to reporters Tuesday morning. “Because I’ve never thrown the challenge flag. Doug [Rosfeld]’s always thrown the challenge flag, and they know that. They ask you that in pregame, ‘who’s got the flag?’ So it’s never been an issue. I didn’t even know it was frowned upon, I guess, and I know that there’s other coaches in the league; I’m not the only one that’s done that.” Tacario “Bobo” Davis, the Bengals’ third-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, has had a solid camp. Geoff Hobson has a nice piece on Davis’ upbringing and where his nickname came from . He’s going against the best wide receiver duo in the NFL in practice, and the Bengals are hoping that’ll transfer to the field. The Bengals will be wearing white jerseys with black pants on Thursday night against the Lions in Preseason Week 1. The starters, or at least most of them, are taking the field to start the 2026 campaign, which includes Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins and Dexter Lawrence. Chase says Joe Burrow looks more aggressive in camp. He likes it. “His demeanor is more aggressive,” Chase said. “His face is more aggressive, the way he talks is more aggressive. He’s got a little mean mug on his face a little bit. I kind of like when he’s like that.” Tahj Brooks has worked on his receiving skills in the offseason. “That’s something I’ve been working on since day one of the offseason and it’s going to show this year,” Brooks said. “Making guys miss in space, being explosive after the catch, and learning all of my routes. It’s a focal point to take another step in this offense.”

title: Browns HC Todd Monken makes his call for QB1 against the Bears
summary: It may have taken longer than he originally expected, but late Wednesday afternoon Todd Monken made the first major decision of his tenure as head coach of the Cleveland Browns. Monken has decided that veteran Deshaun Watson will be the team’s starting quarterback, at least for Saturday’s preseason game against the Chicago Bears. The decision […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - AUGUST 03: Head coach Todd Monken of the Cleveland Browns instructs Deshaun Watson #4 during the Cleveland Browns Training Camp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on August 03, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images It may have taken longer than he originally expected, but late Wednesday afternoon Todd Monken made the first major decision of his tenure as head coach of the Cleveland Browns. Monken has decided that veteran Deshaun Watson will be the team’s starting quarterback, at least for Saturday’s preseason game against the Chicago Bears. The decision ends, at least temporarily, weeks of speculation, debate, and angst over who will be in the offensive huddle for Cleveland’s first offensive possession against the Bears. Do not despair, though, because Shedeur Sanders will also have his turn in Chicago, as Monken said the plan is for both Watson and Sanders to play a half of football on Saturday afternoon to help further the evaluation process : “One’s going to start this week, and one’s going to start next week, and we’re going to play them about a half each. I’d like to see a quarterback play a half and get a two-minute; we’re going to do everything we can to get a two-minute and for the half, and we’re going to try to do the exact same thing the next week.” Given that this appears to be a genuine competition, or at least a competition to confirm what Monken already knows about who the best option is, it probably always made sense that Watson would be the pick. It is a road game, so no fear of the home fans booing Watson, and after not playing since October of 2024, Watson needs some game action against another team. Plus, as Monken pointed out on Wednesday, he had to pick someone to start this week : “You have to pick somebody. I have my reasons for how it’s going to go, and it’s still a competition. We’re excited to watch guys practice today, let alone on Saturday, and then next week against Buffalo, and we’ll get a chance to see them both. “Every week we’ll assess it. It’ll be a little more difficult with the player who doesn’t play as much this week or with the other quarterbacks, right? We’ll be able to assess the quarterback that started and how he played and when the other quarterbacks came in, and then the opposite will be next week against Buffalo.” Since Monken waited until later in the day to make the announcement, there has been no word on how Watson and Sanders are taking the news. But both quarterbacks spoke during the media availability before today’s practice, with Watson saying he’s ready for live football : “For me, it’s just really being able to play live football against a different opponent. I’m not worried about being hit or anything like that. That’s part of the game. But as far as me operating in a live setting without being on the practice field with coaches being on the field with you, that’s what I’m looking forward to, and just getting those reps.” As for Sanders, he is eager to test how much improvement he has made since his rookie season : “I like the challenge of going out there to get the ball out of my hand, so I don’t get hit. That’s the challenge for me, to be able to make the right reads, to be able to go through progressions and figure it out. Even in practice, I don’t take it lightly when I could possibly get hit, because I’m trying to improve the process and speed everything up. It’s extremely tough, but it’s definitely a challenge I look forward to every day going out there.” The quarterback decision, at least for this week, has been made. Even though they are just practice games, it will be good to see both quarterbacks in action as Monken continues to evaluate who the best option will be when the season starts for real on September 13 in Jacksonville.

title: 3 winners, 3 losers from Browns’ training camp
summary: The Cleveland Browns have finished with their training camp portion of the 2026 preseason process. They now go into practices and then compete in three exhibition games. What the coaching staff is gearing up for is the final cutdown on August 30. RELATED: MONKEN TALKS TALENT VERSUS FIT Training camp always reveals so many things. […]
full_text: The Cleveland Browns have finished with their training camp portion of the 2026 preseason process. They now go into practices and then compete in three exhibition games. What the coaching staff is gearing up for is the final cutdown on August 30. RELATED: MONKEN TALKS TALENT VERSUS FIT Training camp always reveals so many things. Certain players who were penciled in as starters suddenly find themselves as a backup when another guy has outplayed him. High-round rookies don’t light up the town as the media and fanbase have assumed they would. Then, out of nowhere, an undrafted veteran or rookie comes along and shines, then makes the final roster. Practice sessions are fair to everyone. Coaches do not care if a guy is a first-or second-round draft pick. They don’t have any reason to shun lesser-known athletes or guys who never heard their name called on draft day. The coaching staff simply wants the best athletes on the field who can do their job. This year’s Browns training camp is different because there is a new head coach, plus many new coaches on his staff. Every year, there are plenty of new faces who just want to play this game and get paid. Certain guys ball out, while others disappoint. Here are three players who used training camp to their advantage, and another three who stood out as riding the disappointment train. WINNERS The rookie receivers Yes, this is a duo instead of just one guy, but this rookie class has already made headlines with both KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston being the offensive stars of camp. Everyone knew that the Browns needed better receivers this year, and GM Andrew Berry snagged a pair with this second and third draft picks. #Browns Shedeur Sanders to Denzel Boston in the end zone pic.twitter.com/P9b61GIRde — Fred Greetham (@FredGreetham9) August 10, 2026 Concepcion has great speed and has been catching everything. Rarely does he drop a ball, and he has been getting in some work as a returner. His burst has really jumped off the screen, and he has great deep speed. Boston’s overall size has been a huge plus, and he knows how to use his long frame. Very good skills in contested catches so far and a crafty route runner. Good blocker as well. OG KT Leveston When Leveston came to the Browns last year, he was projected to be a swing tackle as Cleveland had all of its horses back along the offensive line. Attrition has always been an issue with the Browns, and Bill Callahan wasn’t around to apply Band-Aids, and Leveston was inserted as both Jack Conklin and Dawand Jones fell by the wayside. Leveston did not do well. This year, he has been moved to right guard and has had a very good camp. He is in competition with Teven Jenkins for the starting role. His game has completely reversed itself as he appears steadier and has shown power and solid technique with his long arms, an asset in the middle of the line. His size (6’-4”, 326 pounds) screams offensive tackle, but he has settled in nicely and doesn’t seem to have that air of responsibility like a tackle has. LB Quincy Williams There were major questions when Devin Bush signed elsewhere, but Williams has shown that he and Carson Schwesinger can stop the run and cover tight ends without issue. It seemed that every practice, Williams was making some noteworthy play. He is proving that he will become a force in stopping the run game. He is also a good coverage guy. Williams has shown very good aggression as well. He has good sideline-to-sideline speed, so he is proving to be an every-down backer just like Schwesinger. He is also very physical. He came into camp as a potential candidate who had a lot of experience, but he cemented that he is a capable tackler who should have high tackling numbers. LOSERS WR Jerry Jeudy The coaching staff keeps moving Jeudy around and feels this will free him up by not keeping him in one position and that he can be more successful on the move. But he has been a roller coaster in practices. "Beyond Deshaun Watson maybe not having the best camp so far…Jerry Jeudy continues to struggle with drops. This is not going in the right direction. I'm rooting for him to succeed…this is how you play yourself off a roster." 🚨 @NickWilsonSays and @JPeterlin react to… pic.twitter.com/gr3dTJE8jw — 92.3 The Fan (@923TheFan) August 4, 2026 He is known for drops, and that has continued in this year’s camp. What he needed was a bounce-back development to show that he is still WR1 and these younger guys are complements to his game. However, the exact opposite is happening. The two new young guys, along with veteran Tylan Wallace, are the ones balling out and showing progress. What might help his game is to revert to the short game and leave the long ball to Concepcion. Maybe insert him into the slot instead of outside. But his camp has not been good. Backup cornerbacks This room is in trouble if either Denzel Ward or Tyson Campbell is injured and misses games. Too bad GM Andrew Berry didn’t bring back M. J. Emerson, but the quality just isn’t there this year. Myles Harden holds his own as the nickelback situated in the slot. But the remainder of this room has gotten beaten regularly and often. There are 11 corners in camp. D’Angelo Ross, Michael Coats, and Tre Avery are the ones most widely used behind the starters. Coats is an undrafted rookie and has shown the most of the three, but each one gets fooled by head bob and shoulder shakes. #Browns Shedeur Sanders to KC Concepcion pic.twitter.com/fNyoWkDW8x — Alisson Toro-Lagos 🇨🇱 (@atlTVnews) August 10, 2026 In the above clip, that is Avery trying to stay with Concepcion, and he gets totally juked out of the picture. None of the other corners are in a position to take live snaps on any game day. Former Indianapolis Colts veteran Kenny Moore remains unsigned. Just sayin’. Offensive line So far, the new-look offensive line is more of a who is new in our offensive backfield? Almost every potential starter has had an ailment at some point. The shuffling continues without any real definition of who the five starters are going to be. Center Elgton Jenkins missed sessions due to minor residual soreness, but returned to full squad practice. His backup, Parker Brailsford, has been wearing a brace on his right hand. He was expected to fight for the starting role, but instead has missed valuable time and, upon his return, may end up as the third center now that Luke Wypler has stepped into the backup role. The battle for right guard continues, which is a good thing. Both Teven Jenkins and KT Leveston have gotten their fair share of first-team reps and will solidify this position. At left tackle, it is still undecided between rookie Spencer Fano and Dawand Jones. This might not be decided until the week before the first game. Monken mentioned beefing up on the trenches… Howard is a good choice for that cause — Bread Queen Inoue 🍞👑 (The Calamity is here) (@TheOriginalFla1) March 2, 2026 At right tackle, Tytus Howard has had some nicks of his own. In a recent practice, he walked off the practice field with a trainer, then watched from the sidelines. In his place have been Jones and the rookie Austin Barber, who was penciled in as the backup before Howard’s unknown injury. Injuries occur all over the roster. We get that. But what hasn’t happened with this new lineup on the offensive line is that there is very little cohesiveness going on. Pre-snap penalties are the flavor of the day, as is holding laundry. None of these are working together as one unit. The only player who hasn’t had any issues has been LG Zion Johnson. Everywhere you look, there is an issue. Who are your winners and losers from Browns training camp this year? Share your thoughts with us in the comment section below Join the conversation! title: Browns past vs Browns present: Predicting 2026 sack totals
summary: In one of the offseason’s biggest blockbuster trades, the Cleveland Browns sent Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams in exchange for Jared Verse and several draft picks. Garrett is coming off a career-best 23-sack season, but now that the two players are on different rosters, which one will finish the year with more sacks? It may […]
full_text: In one of the offseason’s biggest blockbuster trades , the Cleveland Browns sent Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams in exchange for Jared Verse and several draft picks. Garrett is coming off a career-best 23-sack season , but now that the two players are on different rosters, which one will finish the year with more sacks? It may be a bold prediction considering Garrett’s Hall of Fame-caliber career and stellar 2025 season, but Verse has a legitimate chance to come out on top in this competition. The young pass rusher finished last season with 7.5 sacks, but with the Browns’ talented defensive line, this should create plenty of opportunities for production. He will be the team’s premier pass rusher on defense. On the other hand, the Rams have Byron Young , who finished last season with 12 sacks, and a potential return from Aaron Donald . If this team has Young, Donald, and Garrett anchoring its defensive line, there are several ways things could play out. Donald and Young could help draw attention from opposing offensive lines, really opening up the opportunity for Garrett to produce at a high level. Alternatively, Young and Donald could split much of the production, potentially leading to lower-than-expected numbers for Garrett. Currently, any sportsbooks that allow betting on sack totals have Garrett as the favorite, especially coming off his record-breaking season, with Verse in the Top 15. Let me know what you think in the comments – who will have more sacks this season: Myles Garrett or Jared Verse? If you just know it’ll be Garrett, how close do you think it will be? full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - AUGUST 10: Philadelphia Eagles tight end Dae'Quan Wright #45 is shown with the ball during the Philadelphia Eagles training camp on August 10th, 2026 at Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cleveland Browns signed big-bodied tight end Dae’Quan Wright out of Ole Miss to bolster the group’s depth. Wright (6’-4”, 255 pounds) is an athletic tight end but has been inconsistent as a blocker. He went undrafted in April’s NFL draft and then signed with the Philadelphia Eagles, but was recently waived. In a corresponding move, the Browns placed CB Damarri Mathis on IR. In Tuesday’s practice, Mathis was carted off the field. Wright began his college career at Virginia Tech and then entered the transfer portal. He chose Ole Miss, where he played the past two seasons. In his college career, he played in 47 games with 113 receptions for 1,603 yards, a 14.2-yard-per-catch average, scored nine touchdowns, averaged 34.1 yards per game, and scored 54 points. In 2025, he was named Second Team All-SEC. Scouting report on Wright on NFL.com : “Wright is a high-cut, tight-hipped tight end who can stretch the field vertically but lacks fluidity and bend for crisp route breaks from speed. He builds speed to threaten defenses, working the vertical limbs of the route tree. He can gain an advantage on linebackers when aligned outside. He’s big and strong enough to improve as a run blocker but needs better technique and commitment in that area. Wright projects as a Day 3 pick who should fight for a role as a TE3/4.“ Currently, the Browns tight end group consists of Harold Fannin, Jack Stoll, Blake Whiteheart, Brenden Bates, and fellow rookies Joe Royer and Ryan Carsen. Royer has not been present during training camp due to what has been described by the team as a personal reason. The Browns will kick off the preseason on Saturday at 1 p.m. on WYTV-33.

title: How the Rams viewed the scrimmage with the Cowboys
summary: The Dallas Cowboys’ defense dominated the headlines coming out of Tuesday’s joint practice with the Rams. Justin Barron intercepted three passes, Dallas generated consistent pressure, and some of the early reviews from the Dallas side were understandably enthusiastic. But what did the other side see? I went through coverage from the The Athletic, ESPN’s Rams […]
full_text: Woodland Hills, CA - August 11:Rams QB Stetson Bennet IV (13) during Rams joint practice with the Dallas Cowboys on Tuesday, August 11, 2026. (Photo by David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys’ defense dominated the headlines coming out of Tuesday’s joint practice with the Rams. Justin Barron intercepted three passes, Dallas generated consistent pressure, and some of the early reviews from the Dallas side were understandably enthusiastic. But what did the other side see? I went through coverage from the The Athletic, ESPN’s Rams coverage, Rams on SI and the Rams’ own website to see what the other side made of Tuesday’s practice. And the picture is more nuanced than some of the Dallas headlines suggest: the Cowboys’ defense made a real impression, but the Rams’ defense won plenty of important battles, too. 1. The Rams’ secondary mostly won the day Nate Atkins of The Athletic explicitly says the Rams’ secondary “ mostly won the day, ” helped by the pass rush. His focus was on how Los Angeles dealt with a Dallas offense loaded with talent at quarterback, running back, receiver and tight end. Los Angeles lived in lots of dime personnel, something it led the league in last season, but it can get more creative and versatile with McDuffie’s ability to play inside and outside, in addition to the growing versatility of Curl and Quentin Lake. McDuffie often slid inside in these settings, offering a second nickel cornerback of sorts to Lake, which threw off the matchups the Cowboys were hunting for by motioning Pickens and Lamb into the slot, or a normal method to expose the lacking coverage of most teams they face. The result was that Dallas didn’t generate many explosive plays. They did generate a couple of yards-after-catch opportunities with dumpoffs to running backs and tight ends in the flat or on play-action leak patterns that tapped into Prescott’s ability to extend the play with his legs. The only time the Cowboys came close to scoring a touchdown was in the red zone period, where Prescott’s dual-threat abilities manipulated the numbers so much that it’s that much harder to get a stop when he can find Ferguson in the back of the end zone, which happened a couple of times. That’s an important counterweight to the Dallas-side narrative. The Cowboys didn’t simply spend the afternoon throwing at an overmatched Rams secondary. 2. Byron Young gave the Cowboys’ tackles problems If there was one Rams defender who consistently caused problems for Dallas, it was Byron Young. Atkins describes Young repeatedly winning against Terence Steele with both speed and power . Byron Young had a field day against Cowboys right tackle Terence Steele. He won with speed around the edge, one time so freely that he actually overran a sack that Prescott turned into a short scramble by dipping around his speeding body. He won with the bull rush at times, including one rep where he drove the pocket back so deep into Prescott that the Cowboys quarterback was left chucking the ball over McDuffie’s tight coverage on the outside just to get it away. He had another rep where he lined up on the left side and threw Guyton into the running back for a quick run stop. The observations from the Rams’ official website similarly highlighted Young’s pressure against Steele and his impact against the run. The fourth-year outside linebacker made it a long morning for Cowboys right tackle Terence Steele. There was one two-play sequence where he led the pass rush generating pressure that collapsed the pocket so fast, it forced Prescott to scramble out of bounds, then Young won so quickly again on the next series he would’ve had a sack if not for the red non-contact jerseys worn by quarterbacks. And all of this happened without Myles Garrett on the field. 3. Dallas forced the Rams to get creative against Pickens and Lamb The Rams weren’t just sitting in their preferred coverage and hoping it would work against Dallas. They were actively adjusting to what the Cowboys were doing with their receivers. Atkins specifically points to Dallas moving CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens into the slot to hunt for favorable matchups. The Rams responded by moving Trent McDuffie inside and using Quentin Lake and Kamren Curl in increasingly versatile roles. In other words, Dallas’ personnel and alignment were forcing the Rams to get creative. The Rams’ own reporting confirms that McDuffie was frequently moved inside during the practice, while Lake operated in a more flexible role. And the day’s biggest Rams coverage play came against Pickens: The Cowboys tried to throw a quick shot to Pickens from the slot, but Lake was all over it, running the route for Pickens and stabbing the ball out of the air before running with it until he was tackled. From the Rams’ perspective, Lake recognized what was coming and made a play. From the Cowboys’ perspective, however, the play confirms that Pickens was being used as a movable piece to stress the Rams’ coverage, rather than simply lining up outside and running routes from the same spot all afternoon. That is probably something worth watching as Dallas continues to develop its offensive identity. 4. Dak’s mobility still gave the Rams problems The Rams’ secondary may have limited the Cowboys’ explosive passing plays, but Atkins repeatedly points to Prescott’s ability to extend plays as a source of success. Dallas created some yards-after-catch opportunities with checkdowns and play-action leaks, but Prescott’s legs were also a factor. And in the red zone, his mobility became particularly difficult for the Rams to account for. Prescott’s dual-threat abilities manipulated the numbers so much that it’s that much harder to get a stop when he can find Ferguson in the back of the end zone, which happened a couple of times. That’s an encouraging detail for Dallas. The Rams could win individual coverage battles and still have a problem because Prescott can turn a broken pocket into a positive play. The L.A. perspective suggests that Dak’s mobility remains a genuine structural problem for opposing defenses. 5. Dallas’ defense genuinely disrupted the Rams’ second-team offense The Cowboys’ three interceptions are the obvious headline, but the L.A. reporting gives us another reason to take the defensive performance seriously. The Rams’ website noted that Dallas’ defensive front consistently generated pressure , particularly against the second-team offense. [Bennett] often received pressure from the Cowboys’ defensive front, but was still able to make plays down the field with a pair of interceptions mixed in by Barron over the middle. The Cowboys’ defense was actually affecting the Rams’ quarterbacks. So what did Los Angeles actually see? The Cowboys did not simply dominate the Rams. But the Rams didn’t dominate Dallas either. The most useful outside perspective may come from Rams on SI , which pushes back against trying to turn the practice into a decisive victory for either side: “the answer is likely somewhere in the middle.” And that is probably the fairest reading of the L.A. coverage. From a Cowboys perspective, the L.A. perspective boils down to four things: Dallas’ defense was legitimately disruptive. The Rams’ own reporting confirms that the Cowboys generated pressure and caused problems for the Rams’ quarterbacks. The Cowboys’ offense created real schematic problems. The Rams adjusted their coverage specifically because Dallas was moving Lamb and Pickens around to create favorable matchups. Dak’s mobility remained a major weapon. Even when the Rams won coverage, Prescott’s ability to extend plays and manipulate numbers created opportunities. The Rams’ defense may be considerably better than last year’s. They limited explosive plays against a Cowboys offense that LA itself considers one of the league’s best — and did it without Myles Garrett. So the most interesting conclusion from the L.A. side isn’t…

title: How the Cowboys can pay George Pickens and still keep their stars
summary: The Cowboys have spent the last two years (mostly) doing exactly what you would expect an NFL team to do: identify their best players and pay them. Dak Prescott (highest-paid QB at signing), CeeDee Lamb (second-highest-paid WR at signing), Tyler Smith (highest-paid iOL at signing), Brandon Aubrey (highest-paid kicker at signing) and now Quinnen Williams […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - NOVEMBER 3: Dallas Cowboys CEO Stephen Jones looks on prior to the game against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on November 3, 2024 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cowboys have spent the last two years (mostly) doing exactly what you would expect an NFL team to do: identify their best players and pay them. Dak Prescott (highest-paid QB at signing), CeeDee Lamb (second-highest-paid WR at signing), Tyler Smith (highest-paid iOL at signing), Brandon Aubrey (highest-paid kicker at signing) and now Quinnen Williams (second-highest-paid iDL). Dallas has handed out top-of-the-market contracts to all five. And that’s the right thing to do. NFL teams don’t win by deliberately letting their best players walk. Either trade them (Micah Parsons) or pay them (see above). The problem is that NFL teams don’t get unlimited credit for identifying good players. Eventually, they have to fit those players under the salary cap. So the interesting question isn’t whether the Cowboys can afford to pay their stars. It’s whether they can keep finding enough good players cheaply enough to afford the stars they already have. And that’s where the draft becomes much more than a talent-acquisition exercise. You can’t pay everyone Let’s start with a simple thought experiment. There are five positions that sit at the extreme ends of the passing game: the guy who throws the ball (QB), the guy who chases the guy who throws the ball (DE), the guy who best catches the ball (WR), the guy who covers the guy catching the ball best (CB), and the guy who blocks for the guy throwing the ball (OT) – the Money 5. If you build a roster around one top-of-market player at each of those positions and use the 2026 franchise tag as a proxy for what those players cost, here’s the bill: body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 0px 6px !important; } Position 2026 Franchise Tag Quarterback $43.9 million Wide Receiver $27.3 million Offensive Lineman (LT) $25.8 million Defensive End $24.4 million Cornerback $21.2 million Total “Money 5” $142.6 million 2026 Salary Cap $301.2 million “Money 5” in % of Cap 47% The franchise tag isn’t a realistic way to build a roster, of course. But it is a useful proxy for the cost of having a top-of-market player at each position. And those five players alone consume 47% of the salary cap. In reality, you’d probably spend more than 50%, because the franchise tag is a lagging indicator based on previous-year salaries, while the actual market keeps moving upward. Which means that before you’ve even started filling out the rest of the roster, roughly half your salary cap is gone. And that’s only five players. Ten stars would eat almost the entire cap Let’s extend the exercise. If you’re building a roster around the positions that have the biggest influence on the passing game, you probably don’t stop at one receiver or one pass rusher. Add a second wide receiver, a second offensive lineman. And then plug in more defenders: a defensive tackle, another defensive end, and a safety. Now you have a 10-player Franchise Tag Team. Here’s what that team would have cost over the last five years: body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 0px 6px !important; } Tag by position in $M 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 Quarterback 29.7 32.4 38.3 42.5 43.9 Wide Receiver I 18.4 19.7 21.3 24.8 27.3 Offensive Lineman I 16.7 18.2 21.0 24.7 25.8 Defensive End I 17.9 20.9 24.0 24.3 24.4 Cornerback 17.3 18.1 19.8 20 21.2 Wide Receiver II 18.4 19.7 21.8 24.8 27.3 Defensive Tackle 17.4 18.9 22.1 22.4 27.2 Offensive Lineman II 16.7 18.2 21.0 24.7 25.8 Defensive End II 17.9 19.7 21.8 24.3 24.4 Safety 12.9 14.5 17.1 18.6 20.1 Grand Total 183.3 200.3 228.2 251.1 267.4 Salary Cap 208.2 224.8 255.4 279.2 301.2 Top 10 in% of cap 88% 89% 89% 90% 89% And here’s the uncomfortable part: This isn’t some unusual 2026 phenomenon. Whether you run the calculation using the 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, or 2026 salary cap, the answer barely moves – Ten top-of-market players would consume roughly 89% of the cap. The numbers, in sequence, are 88%, 89%, 89%, 90%, and 89%, respectively. So, no, you can’t build an NFL roster by paying ten players the going rate for elite talent. At 2026 prices, you’d have about $34 million left to pay 43 additional players. The math simply doesn’t work. Unless, of course, some of those ten players aren’t actually costing you $20-30 million. And that’s where the draft comes in. The 4-and-6 model This is the fundamental value of the rookie contract. Suppose four of those ten players are still on rookie deals, costing perhaps $4-6 million each rather than the roughly $26 million average you’d pay at the top of their respective markets. Suddenly, you’ve shaved roughly $80 million off the cost of your top ten players. That’s not a minor salary-cap advantage. That’s the mechanism that makes the entire roster possible. In a healthy roster-building cycle, you want something like six established players getting paid at or near market rates, while four of your best players are still providing production on cheap rookie contracts. The draft, therefore, isn’t simply a way to acquire talent. It’s a way to replace expensive talent with inexpensive talent before the salary cap forces you to choose between them. And that means draft misses are particularly costly. If a rookie fails to become the player you expected, you don’t simply lose the value of that draft pick. You may eventually have to replace that player with an expensive veteran. That replacement inevitably costs more. The cap space disappears. And suddenly, you have less flexibility to keep somebody else. That’s the roster-building cycle the Cowboys, like any other team, have to manage. Where the Cowboys stand So, how does Dallas look through this 4-and-6 lens? Let’s take the same 10 positions and look at both the players’ 2026 cap hits and the average annual value (AAV) of their contracts. body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 0px 6px !important; } POS Player 2026 Cap Hit in $M AAV in $M Quarterback Dak Prescott 44.6 60.0 Wide Receiver I George Pickens 27.3 27.3 Offensive Lineman I Tyler Guyton 3.6 3.3 Defensive End I Rashan Gary 5.7 16.0 Cornerback Daron Bland 17 22.5 Wide Receiver II CeeDee Lamb 19.7 34.0 Defensive Tackle Quinnen Williams 21.6 30.6 Offensive Lineman II Tyler Smith 10.3 21.3 Defensive End II Donovan Ezeiruaku 3.4 2.5 Safety Caleb Downs 5.3 7.2 Grand Total 158.5 224.7 In % of cap 48% 68% At first glance, this looks pretty good. The Cowboys’ Top 10 account for only 48% of their 2026 cap. But that’s the difference between what the contracts cost and when the Cowboys have chosen to pay for them . Based on AAV, the Cowboys have committed the equivalent of 68% of the 2026 salary cap to these ten players. The lower 2026 cap-hit number is the product of restructures, pushed-out cap charges, and, increasingly, void years added to the contracts. Dak Prescott is the clearest example. His contract carries an average value of $60 million per year, but Dallas has pushed money into future seasons to create current-year cap room. That gives the Cowboys flexibility today, but it doesn’t make the money disappear. It simply changes when the bill comes due. And that’s why the cheap players matter so much. Dallas is short one…

title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 32
summary: It is Day 32 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like […]
full_text: Football: NFC Playoffs: Dallas Cowboys QB Danny White (11) in action vs Atlanta Falcons at Texas Stadium. Irving, TX 12/30/1978 CREDIT: Walter Iooss Jr. (Photo by Walter Iooss Jr. /Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) (Set Number: X23016 TK1 R13 F37 ) It is Day 32 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. Here it is, Day 32 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, and we revisit a playoff victory that tested the Cowboys’ experience, depth and ability to overcome mistakes. Dallas committed four turnovers and lost Roger Staubach to an injury before halftime, but Danny White steadied the offense and the defense shut out Atlanta in the second half to secure a divisional-round win. Saturday, December 30, 1978 — 4:00 p.m. ET Texas Stadium, Irving, Texas Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 27, Atlanta Falcons 20 The defending Super Bowl champions finished 12-4 and won the NFC East entering the postseason. Atlanta had gone 9-7 before defeating Philadelphia in the first Wild Card round introduced under the NFL’s expanded playoff format. Despite not being expected to eliminate Dallas, the Falcons’ aggressive defense and physical running game quickly made the afternoon uncomfortable. Rafael Septién opened the scoring with a 34-yard field goal, followed by Bubba Bean’s 14-yard touchdown run to put Atlanta ahead. Dallas responded with a creative drive, featuring White gaining 12 yards on a fake punt and Scott Laidlaw breaking a 21-yard run. Laidlaw then completed the possession with a 13-yard touchdown, giving the Cowboys a 10-7 lead. Atlanta dominated the second quarter, thanks in part to a muffed Dallas punt that set up Tim Mazzetti’s tying field goal. However, Septién restored the Cowboys’ advantage from 48 yards. Despite this, the Falcons scored 10 unanswered points, including a Steve Bartkowski touchdown pass to Wallace Francis and another Mazzetti field goal. Dallas’s troubles continued, with three fumbles by halftime and Staubach being knocked out of the game after a heavy hit from linebacker Robert Pennywell. As a result, Atlanta entered the break leading 20-13. White’s big moment in relief nearly turned into a nightmare when an interception handed Dallas their fourth turnover of the day. But the veteran Cowboys defense refused to break, slamming the door on Atlanta and forcing a punt. Blessed with great field position, White got his shot at redemption, and he didn’t waste it. He fired a 24-yard strike to Billy Joe DuPree, sliced off another 15 yards to Scott Laidlaw, and capped off the march by finding Jackie Smith in the end zone for a two-yard touchdown. Just like that, we had a brand new ballgame tied at 20. The Cowboys’ defense then chose the exact right moment to suffocate the Falcons. Aaron Kyle came up with a massive interception on a tipped Bartkowski pass, and a 20-yard end-around by DuPree put Dallas in business. They came up empty on that drive, but the pressure was clearly getting to Atlanta, whose next short punt handed Dallas the ball on the Falcons’ 30-yard line. With victory in sight, Scott Laidlaw pounded the rock, scoring his second touchdown of the game from one yard out to push Dallas ahead 27-20. Despite having opportunities to respond, the Falcons were unable to overcome the Cowboys. Late in the fourth quarter, they reached Dallas territory, but the Cowboys stopped them on fourth-and-one. With only 59 seconds remaining, Atlanta received one final possession, but Cliff Harris intercepted Bartkowski, ending the comeback attempt. This game belongs on the countdown because Dallas found a way to advance despite almost everything going wrong before halftime. The Cowboys lost their starting quarterback, repeatedly gave Atlanta short fields and committed four turnovers, but their veteran defense refused to allow another point. White then provided enough composure off the bench to complete the comeback. #Cowboys vs #Falcons 1978 Divisional Round Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 27, Atlanta Falcons 20 #DallasCowboys #NFL (📽️: @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/o30BZoVPPX — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) August 12, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game This was the first postseason meeting between the Cowboys and Falcons, and they would meet one more time in 1980. Since then the two teams have never played each other in the playoffs. title: Cowboys begin to answer big questions in scrimmage at Rams
summary: Step number one of two is complete for the week when it comes to the Dallas Cowboys competing against the NFC West, the division with the best winning percentage in football a season ago. The Cowboys visited Los Angeles to scrimmage against the Rams on Tuesday, and the football-ism that defense travels applied for Christian […]
full_text: Step number one of two is complete for the week when it comes to the Dallas Cowboys competing against the NFC West, the division with the best winning percentage in football a season ago. The Cowboys visited Los Angeles to scrimmage against the Rams on Tuesday, and the football-ism that defense travels applied for Christian Parker’s defense going up against Sean McVay’s offense. Step number two of this week’s journey will be the preseason opener at the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. Before fully turning the page into that matchup, let’s take a deeper look at how the Cowboys matched up with the Rams. The loudest noise coming out of this scrimmage was made by the Dallas defense, in some very key areas when it comes to questions we had about the defense and the answers they showed. Since before the draft, what the Cowboys were going to do about the true linebacker position, and not the outside pass rushing linebacker spot, has been a major question. Through all of the recent scheme changes, this has likely been the position that’s gone through the most turmoil with wildly different philosophies about what the LB personnel should look like. Let’s face it, this group hit rock bottom under Matt Eberflus last year, and was likely the face of the historically bad 2025 defense, with linebackers getting completely torched in coverage and missing tackles/taking bad angles in the run game being a snap-by-snap occurrence. The concern level was so high at linebacker that some draft projections had the Cowboys taking a player like CJ Allen or Jacob Rodriguez. Instead, the Cowboys waited until the 92nd overall pick to add a tweener-type linebacker Jaishawn Barham, who didn’t even participate in the Rams scrimmage, and introduced the world to Justin Barron while also seeing Dee Winters start to assert himself. The Cowboys are really maximizing what they have to work with on defense right now under this new coaching staff, and that showed against the Rams. Barron had three interceptions on the day, becoming the latest player to help prove that Christian Parker is on a whole different level of defensive masterminding for the Cowboys in his first year (and first ever time) as a defensive coordinator. Parker has embraced working with players that were already here before his hiring, even at the undrafted free agent level like with Barron, as well as safety Julius Wood. Julius Wood has made a couple of key plays, including a PBU on a slant from Stafford. https://t.co/WnnJyYU6Z6 — Patrik [No C] Walker (@VoiceOfTheStar) August 11, 2026 Dallas has also stepped out of their normal comfort zone to hand pick scheme-specific fits for Parker, and this Rams scrimmage helped prove that the depth chart on defense doesn’t just look drastically different from a year ago, it feels and most importantly plays different. The way players with potential in the secondary are also hitting the ground running under Parker’s coaching, like Shavon Revel Jr. and Caleb Downs, checks an early box that defense can be a positive factor. Revel finished plays against the Rams, which is a great sign for so many reasons. First and foremost, it was exactly what Parker recently said he was looking for in the next steps of the year two cornerback’s development. Second, it makes us feel good about the Cowboys star-studded receiving group, as they’ve been the ones consistently finishing catches against Revel in drills, but that didn’t last against the Rams. Watched the Cowboys defense in the first team period. No big plays allowed. Shavon Revel with a PBU on deep ball from Stafford to Nacua stood out. — Todd Archer (@toddarcher) August 11, 2026 With Barron and Winters patrolling the middle of the field, and the Cowboys having a plethora of players that can interchange between the second and third level like Wood, Markquese Bell, Caleb Downs, and Alijah Clark, as well as showing plenty of pass rush juice off the edge against the Rams, this defense is out full force to confuse opposing offenses from the jump in 2026. Christian Parker is scheming his ass off rn in #Cowboys joint practice vs Rams. multiple first-team *sacks* (3 so far) + two INTs + run defense is shutting down the RBs entirely. i am IMPRESSED. 🔬🔥 — Patrik [No C] Walker (@VoiceOfTheStar) August 11, 2026 The next positive updates to look for in these terms would be splash plays from the likes of Shemar James and DeMarvion Overshown, with the latter being impressed by the progress the Cowboys made on Tuesday against the Rams compared to last training camp’s scrimmage against them, which happened in Oxnard. Cowboys LB DeMarvion Overshown on if they saw this joint practice as a litmus test for the defense: “We just looked at it as another opportunity to get better. We know Matt Stafford is one of the best in the business, that wide receiving corps, and then those running backs and… https://t.co/0MVXuMFoxb — Nick Harris (@NickHarrisFWST) August 12, 2026 The Rams’ own defensive line is going to be a handful for every team they play this season, one that will feature Myles Garrett, who the Cowboys did not have to deal with on Tuesday. This Rams front still gave the Cowboys offensive line enough trouble to make it – by all reports – a bit of a tough day for the offense. The interior run game did not gain the traction it had in team drills previously, and a result of this was the play-action game not looking quite sharp yet. To go straight from competing against your own teammates and having to hold back a certain level of physicality to avoid injury to a scrimmage setting against a team as physical as the Rams is no easy feat. Come Saturday, the Cowboys offense likely won’t even be playing many of the starters that did get some work against the Rams. Offensive coordinator Klayton Adams called the plays in this scrimmage, and will likely be looking for the fundamental takeaways in technique and execution he can pass down to the depth players that will get the most run against the Seahawks. When the Cowboys pass pro did hold up against the Rams though, there were some big plays in the pass game, including this acrobatic catch by rookie WR Anthony Smith. WATCH: Anthony Smith makes the one-handed grab on the run for the Cowboys in Tuesday's practice with the Rams. 📹 Dallas Cowboys #piratesinthepros 🏴‍☠️ pic.twitter.com/R3IszgkDsX — Pirate Radio ☠️ (@PR927FM) August 11, 2026 We already highlighted Smith before this scrimmage as a player needing a strong start to the preseason, and how getting separation from defenders to show off his speed would go the longest way. Smith did just that against the Rams, and now will carry even more excitement into Saturday. UDFA TE Michael Trigg also caught another touchdown in Tuesday’s work, something that should make the Rams coaching staff smirk seeing how other teams are embracing their approach to throwing multiple athletic freaks at tight end on the field at the same time. Slowly but steadily, Trigg is nearing the point where there is consistent enough buzz about him to put a big circle around his name ahead of Saturday’s exhibition, and see if he can take yet another step to make the TE depth competition super interesting. Who knows, by the time Week 15 rolls around and the Cowboys are visiting the Rams for real, they could be lining up similarly on offense with three capable tight ends – and Trigg being that third guy behind Jake Ferguson and Brevyn Spann-Ford. Spann-Ford also stood out in the scrimmage with a touchdown of his own. Not allowed to take video from the Cowboys and Rams practice. title: 5 takeaways from the Cowboys vs Rams scrimmage
summary: On Tuesday against the Los Angeles Rams, the Dallas Cowboys showed that the buzz around them to start training camp shouldn’t be looked at as a mirage. The Dallas offense and defense won their fair share of battles against Los Angeles and weren’t just bulldozed like they were when the Rams visited Oxnard, CA last […]
full_text: Aug 11, 2026; Woodland Hills, CA, USA; Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer reacts during a joint practice against the Los Angeles Rams at the Rams Practice Facility. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect On Tuesday against the Los Angeles Rams, the Dallas Cowboys showed that the buzz around them to start training camp shouldn’t be looked at as a mirage. The Dallas offense and defense won their fair share of battles against Los Angeles and weren’t just bulldozed like they were when the Rams visited Oxnard, CA last year. After taking a day to comb through the social media notes and practice recaps from beat reporters, here are some of the biggest next-day thoughts to take from the Cowboys-Rams scrimmage and what it means moving forward: Tyler Guyton continues to build confidence With all 11 starters returning on offense for Dallas, there weren’t many question marks heading into training camp like there were in 2025. The most important question that needed to be answered is where Tyler Guyton is in his development. Tuesday should give fans hope that things continue to move in the right direction. Guyton was praised by many for how he handled the Rams edge players when they rushed the quarterback and in the run game. Granted, Myles Garrett was watching from the sidelines, so Guyton wasn’t tested by the best pass rusher in the league. However, it’s still positive to hear that Guyton not only looks stronger after his work this offseason, but is taking the positive reps we’ve seen in camp and bringing them over to face other competition. Terence Steele has to fix some things On the opposite side, Terence Steele did not have a great day against the Rams. On 105.3 The Fan , Voch Lombardi talked about what he saw from the Cowboys right tackle and it wasn’t a glowing review. Is it a five-alarm fire? It shouldn’t be because Byron Young is the Rams’ second-best pass rusher next to Garrett. However, a team’s second-best rusher can’t look like an All-Pro if the Cowboys are looking to replicate what they did last year on offense. Maybe in passing situations this year, the Cowboys keep Brevyn Spann-Ford tied to the hip pocket of Steele to chip the rusher and allow him to get an extra step on a defender. At the end of the day, Terence Steele might be the offensive line’s fifth-best lineman, and that’s okay. As long as the Cowboys aren’t naïve to that fact and can game plan accordingly on game day, it should be fine. Steele has a few more weeks to show Tuesday’s practice was just a blip. Is the Justin Barron hype real? Maybe it was the inspiration from Luke Kuechly being inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame over the weekend that caused Justin Barron to have a breakout scrimmage. The second-year, undrafted linebacker had not one, not two, but three interceptions against the Rams. One of them came against the starters and Matthew Stafford. What does that mean moving forward? Well, Barron has been in a rotation at linebacker for all of camp with the second- and third-team defense. The top three backers on the team are pretty much set in DeMarvion Overshown, Dee Winters, and Jaishawn Barham. However, the fourth and potential fifth spots are open for grabs. Curtis Robinson, a veteran who was signed before camp, was getting reps with the second team as the Mike linebacker in Barham’s absence. Having a capable backup at that spot is too important for Christian Parker’s defense, so if Robinson is being trusted with those duties, it might give him the leg up in spot No. 4. That means Barron might be fighting with Shemar James for that final spot in the linebacker room. James has the draft capital invested in him as a second-year player who led the team in tackles as a rookie. However, James hasn’t shown up in practice the way Barron did on Tuesday. The biggest test will come in the preseason games, and both James and Barron will get every opportunity to play. Then we’ll know for sure if Barron is another home run from undrafted free agency or if he’s another training camp darling at linebacker. The Cowboys dynamic trio It was a back-and-forth scrimmage from both offenses, but the highlights from CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, and Ryan Flournoy can make for some scary acquisitions. Not in a bad way. Like in a “Do the Cowboys have the best trio of wideouts in the NFL?” kind of way. had some fun in the LA sun ☀️ #CowboysCamp | @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/Ba4J7ucZeK — Dallas Cowboys (@dallascowboys) August 11, 2026 Lamb and Flournoy found the end zone while Pickens was terrorizing Rams defenders all day. The Cowboys have clearly been working on their red zone offense in training camp, as it was the one black mark on their stellar performance from 2025. Dallas’ red zone efficiency was near the bottom half of the league at 56.9 percent. In a tight-quarters situation like playing in the red zone usually is, Brian Schottenheimer needs answers. If Pickens is going to be doubled down there, then Lamb and Flournoy need to win one-on-one. If all three are blanketed one-on-one, then Jake Ferguson needs to beat the linebacker or safety that’s rolling in his direction. The offensive retreat to Park City, UT seems to be paying dividends for the Cowboys offense in training camp. On Tuesday, it was just another reason to buy into the hype around Dallas’ dynamic trio and how they can bring this offense to even greater heights than where they were last year. Brian Schottenheimer’s culture is growing To close out practice, the Cowboys got together for some extra conditioning. Schottenheimer has been having Dallas run sprints at the end of practice, not for disciplinary reasons, but to get his guys ready for the long season and be the best-conditioned team in the NFL. Schottenheimer has also talked about his mission to build the best culture in American sports. On Tuesday, it was a blending of the two. Dak Prescott told the media that he and DeMarvion Overshown came together and got the offense and defense to do the extra conditioning. This wasn’t something Schottenheimer made the call on; it was a player-driven move. One could look at it and say it’s corny for Dallas to do it in front of the Rams as they’re walking off the field, but the bigger takeaway should be that Schottenheimer’s culture is now self-sustaining. Players taking the lead and doing this on their own shows everything he’s trying to build in Dallas is working and that the team is buying into it. If they didn’t do their usual conditioning after practice, or only half the team did it, it would raise some eyebrows. In this case, it showcases that things are coming together as a team in Dallas. The Cowboys got in some cardio after practice to the surprise of the snickering Rams players. George Pickens told the Rams to keep walking and mind their own business. Dont even look over here, he said. The conditioning after practice was player led. Not prompted by coaches.… pic.twitter.com/PWzTeWcwjr — Clarence Hill Jr (@clarencehilljr) August 11, 2026
