title: Eagles News: Jonathan Greenard expected to miss “another couple of weeks, at least”
summary: Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Jonathan Greenard will miss “another couple weeks at least” for Eagles – PFTEagles linebacker Jonathan Greenard has not practiced yet at training camp and it will still be some time before he’s ready to get on the field. Greenard is on the physically unable to […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - MAY 27: Jonathan Greenard #52 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during OTA offseason workouts at Jefferson Health Training Complex on May 27, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Jonathan Greenard will miss “another couple weeks at least” for Eagles – PFT Eagles linebacker Jonathan Greenard has not practiced yet at training camp and it will still be some time before he’s ready to get on the field. Greenard is on the physically unable to perform list due to a pectoral injury and defensive coordinator Vic Fangio said at a Tuesday press conference that it will be “another couple weeks at least” before he’s able to resume football activities. Fangio said that the extended time off is something the Eagles will have to keep in mind as they try to avoid further injury once Greenard has returned to action. Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Uar Bernard is showing some promise – BGN CB Quinyon Mitchell went to the ground after getting tangled up with Hollywood Brown in WR vs. DB 1-on-1 drills. Mitchell was slow to get up and spent some time on one knee with a trainer. He did not participate in team drills but he also did not visit the medical tent or leave the practice field early, so, those are some encouraging signs. Eagles training camp player stock up/stock down media poll – PhillyVoice 1) Darius Cooper: 14 votes … 2) Jalyx Hunt: 3 votes … 3) Willie Lampkin: 2 votes … For full disclosure, my vote was for Darius Cooper, who began camp on the roster bubble, but who has played his way into consideration for a starting job. Obviously, he ran away with the vote here. Four other players got one vote each. In alphabetical order: QB Jalen Hurts, iOL Drew Kendall, WR Elijah Moore, LB Jeremiah Trotter. I agree that Hunt, Lampkin, Hurts, Kendall, Moore, and Trotter have all had good camps. Camp Notes – Good Depth – Iggles Blitz The Eagles know as well as anyone that you need depth if you want to win in the NFL, where the season isa war of attrition. With that said, lets talk about some key backups. OL depth is critical, as the team saw last year when Cam Jurgens and Landon Dickerson shouldn’t have been on the field. Drew Kendall was a rookie last season and focused on learning. Now he’s the top backup on the inside and could play if needed. 2026 NFL offensive line rankings: Broncos, Eagles and Buccaneers open in top three – PFF 2) PHILADELPHIA EAGLES. The big change on the offensive line for the Eagles this season is the departure of former offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland, but like the Broncos in the top spot, they return the same starting five. Right tackle Lane Johnson has indicated that this is likely to be his last season in the NFL, so we only have one more year to marvel at one of the finest pass blockers to play in the NFL since PFF began grading. Johnson has earned a PFF pass-blocking grade above 80.0 in six straight seasons and allowed just seven total pressures from 262 pass-blocking snaps a year ago. The ‘little secret weapon’ who keeps turning heads at Eagles training camp – NBCSP At just 5-foot-11 and just 290 pounds, Willie Lampkin doesn’t look like an NFL offensive lineman. Until he starts to play. Because it has become clear over the last couple of weeks that Lampkin is an NFL player and he’s pushing extremely hard for a spot on the Eagles’ 53-man roster. He has been turning the heads of his teammates and coaches along the way. “I think Willie’s done a phenomenal job,” starting left guard Landon Dickerson said. “He plays with great leverage, great feet. He’s a strong guy. He’s kind of like our little secret weapon when it comes to the D-linemen. I just don’t think he’s your typical size for an offensive lineman, which can be a game-changer going against defensive linemen.” Eagles QB Jalen Hurts’ speed in camp drawing rave reviews – ESPN Quarterback Jalen Hurts’ speed has been standing out at Eagles’ training camp, and members of the defense are taking notice. “I think Jalen’s having a good camp. I think he looks faster,” said defensive coordinator Vic Fangio. “Obviously we can’t touch him during practice so there’s always that debate whether you had him or not [for a sack] and I think there’s been a few times where our guys think they had him and they really didn’t.” Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jalen Carter agrees. He came into training camp about 10 pounds lighter but is still having a hard time catching up to QB1. “I don’t know what it is but when I’m watching and I’m running [after him], it’s like a movie, it feels like I’m going slow,” Carter said. “He be moving man, he’s been working hard and he’s the one, for sure.” NFL Power Rankings: Rams enter preseason on top; Seahawks at No. 3, Patriots outside top 10 – NFL.com 4) PHILADELPHIA EAGLES. It might seem shocking to see the Eagles land at such a lofty place. That’s fair, especially given how poorly they performed in the latter portion of the 2025 season. Things seem different with this team now, though, starting with the vibes. Everyone seems happier — with the scheme directed by new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion, with the standard of accountability being emphasized within the building, and with some of the additions made on both sides of the ball. Jonathan Greenard’s absence (pec strain) is concerning but doesn’t leave the kind of gaping hole that such an injury would create on lesser teams. There’s plenty to sort out with this new-look receiving corps, too, but after moving on from the drama that seemed to follow A.J. Brown, I trust this steadily competitive franchise to produce a better offense, pair it with a talented defense and make another run at an NFC East crown (and more). Spadaro: The adaptive Johnny Mundt – PhiladelphiaEagles.com The role, as developed during the course of a career now in its 11th season, is to win at the line of scrimmage. Mundt has 74 career catches – his most, 19, in the 2022 and 2024 seasons with Minnesota – but he has made it in this league because he’s a great blocking tight end. He won Super Bowl LVI with the Rams and played for the Jaguars before signing with the Eagles this offseason. You do what you have to do. “A lot of point of attack blocking, making plays in the fast game, obviously. Just being a multi-dimensional tight end and just helping out any way I can,” Mundt said about what he can bring to the Eagles’ offense. Being attached to the line of scrimmage, being point of attack on a lot of these blocks, you can do a lot of play action … and again, the marriage of the run of the pass has been core to this offense ever since its start.” The tush push meets ‘Madden’: How EA Sports added the notorious play to the video game – The Athletic Yes, the tush push — the quarterback sneak that the Eagles popularized and a majority of NFL teams fought to ban — is coming to “Madden.” A year after Philadelphia won the Super Bowl and Saquon Barkley hurdled his way onto the game’s cover, the Eagles’ signature play will be a key addition to this year’s game, “Madden NFL 27,” which will be released Thursday. Tush push in EA Sports’ ‘Madden NFL 27’ Typically, installing new plays or features in “Madden” requires two or three players to simulate the action while wearing motion-capture equipment. But to imitate the nuances of the tush push — which is distinguished from a regular QB sneak by teammates shoving the ball carrier forward — EA needed a bigger production and an extra level of intensity, including motion-capture sessions that Boatright described with the enthusiasm of a coach in the heat of training camp. “(It was) a mindset of, ‘I have to wreak havoc,’ if I’m on defense,” Boatright said, “or, if I’m on the offensive side, ‘I’ve got to put this guy in the dirt.’ “We want to make sure we mimic everything that happens in real life as often as we possibly can.” Eagles Eye Mobile gives free eye exams and glasses to local…

title: Steelers mailbag: Rookies, Big Mike McCarthy, and future QBs
summary: The Steelers play football tomorrow! With the preseason just a day away at this point, Read & React is back with our promised mailbag column ahead of Thursday night’s kickoff. In late July, we asked for some questions about the team, and you all delivered. I’m also happy to announce that, due to the few […]
full_text: Aug 03, 2026; Latrobe, PA, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy talks with quarterback Aaron Rodgers (8) during a practice session at Training camp at Saint Vincent College. Mandatory Credit: Barry Reeger-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Steelers play football tomorrow! With the preseason just a day away at this point, Read & React is back with our promised mailbag column ahead of Thursday night’s kickoff. In late July, we asked for some questions about the team, and you all delivered. I’m also happy to announce that, due to the few questions we got about training camp, we brought in contributor Joey Bray, who has been covering training camp for BTSC, to help us out with this column. Let’s dive in: Polamolecules_Dude : After seeing so many rankings for the Steelers (WRs, etc) being ranked so low, how realistic are these rankings with a whole new coaching staff and many new players? Is it just because of so many changes, or nobody really knowing what to expect from this team? Is that maybe a good thing? RB : Without real football to fall back on, the summer becomes ranking season for much of the media, and we’ve kept tabs on quite a few of the more prominent lists here at BTSC. Ryan and I even devoted a column to discussing whether Pittsburgh was being disrespected by the national media based on where the Black and Gold have been falling in power rankings as of late (I said the Steelers are possibly underrated, but not egregiously so). Regarding the last part of your question, is it a good thing? Maybe. Some athletes are always looking for a little bit of motivation, and I’m sure rankings articles can supply that, but there hasn’t been much noise about that beyond fanbase and media chatter. But although I think it’s fair to argue the team ranking can be low in the preseason lists, the player rankings have largely been reasonable. And I can say that while still being a bit more optimistic regarding the roster than the national media. Simply put, the Steelers are a roster in transition. A lot of the big names have aged out of their prime, but while the tired narrative of an “old roster” is somewhat accurate in regards to the team’s star players, it doesn’t properly represent the overall roster. Sure, many of the young, upcoming names — which are often forgotten in that narrative — haven’t truly reached stardom yet. But that still leaves Pittsburgh with a surprisingly solid roster from top to bottom, even if it has few consensus “top 10” names. I’m not sure if that has much to do with uncertainty regarding the new coaching staff, which, if anything, has seemingly increased the optimism around how the Steelers can maximize talent on both sides of the ball. But there is definitely plenty of uncertainty regarding whether those older players can keep fighting off Father Time, and whether the younger names can keep their upward trajectories. As for the main part of your question, I don’t think the rankings are particularly realistic or unrealistic — frankly, even the best of us fail to accurately predict much of each upcoming NFL season. As players such as Zach Frazier, Joey Porter Jr., Troy Fautanu, Nick Herbig and Darnell Washington continue to stack strong seasons, they’ll probably start to get more national hype and I’m willing to bet the Steelers see one or two more players on ESPN’s top-10 lists heading into next season, even as names such as TJ Watt and Cam Heyward start to fade out of the spotlight. To your point, though, there are plenty of unknowns with this team, and I can’t wait to move from the endless speculation to the “real football” part of the year, which kicks off tomorrow for Steelers fans. Still, well-put-together rankings can be an interesting look at how the team compares to the rest of the league. Check out Bleacher Report’s Brandon Thorn’s informative offensive line ranking (which was bullish on some Steelers) for a strong example. CT-Steeler4Life : Now that the Steelers have gone out of their comfort zone and hired a 62-year-old head coach (Austin and Noll were 47 and Cowher and Tomlin were 43 when hired), how long do you predict McCarthy sticks around? If he can’t work wonders with this current quarterback room, which everyone thinks he’s good at, I believe that after 2 seasons, Steelers Nation will be calling for his replacement. Which young head coach candidate is your preference for the long-term future? RP : I was skeptical about the McCarthy hire when it happened. Hands up to the sky, full transparency here: I am the guy who wrote the opinion piece on why hiring McCarthy would be a mistake . Like you, most of my arguments against that decision were tied to the long-term potential of hiring a 62-year-old coach taking on his third head coaching gig. Those concerns are certainly still in the back of my mind when I take the big-picture view of this club’s future. But I must admit, I have found most of the reports from OTAs and now training camp to be a breath of fresh air. I am still thankful for Mike Tomlin’s contributions over the years, but regular readers of this column know that both Ryland and I were ready to see some new ideas and voices take over for a team that had grown stagnant. We are all familiar with the various complaints about how this team has been run in recent years, and I don’t particularly feel like litigating them again is useful or necessary at this point. But I will say that the staff McCarthy has surrounded himself with gives me some optimism. The players brought in during free agency and through the draft mostly make sense. I may still believe the end result for the Steelers will be similar, but I’m encouraged that steps are being taken to address some of the team’s longest-standing concerns. Players, like Keeanu Benton, are being asked to play positions that fit them more naturally than the miscastings they were forced into and stubbornly held to by the old regime. I have a growing confidence that both the offense and defense will make adjustments that make sense. I’m willing to keep an open mind and give McCarthy a chance to let things play out. I think Year 1 will be about building a foundation, and next season will be when we can really start to evaluate if he is capable of being the bridge to the future this organization needs. To answer your questions more directly, I think barring a total catastrophe, McCarthy will serve no less than four years of the five-year deal he was given. After all, this was an organization that, by all reports, was willing to run it back with Tomlin again had he not resigned. Next year the team will either draft a quarterback or make a play for a veteran and perhaps see how far Drew Allar has progressed after a year in the building. In all likelihood, McCarthy will finish his contract unless he decides to step away for any of the many reasons a man in his 60s might decide to. The second part of your question is then likely impossible to predict. This cycle I was really high on Jesse Minter, and was then, of course, disgusted when he predictably signed with the rival Ravens. But predicting who might be a coaching candidate five years from now is pure speculation. Could a coach like Kyle Shanahan follow an Andy Reid-type career path where he leaves his first team and finally gets over the hump with team two? Could a clearly talented coach like Demeco Ryans be available if the Texans don’t win it all with their elite defense? Guessing which current position coaches will rise to head coaching candidates is likely an exercise in futility. What I will say is I respect adaptability in a coach. I like coaches who aren’t satisfied to stick with one system or scheme regardless of what roster they have or what changes are happening around the league. Whoever eventually follows McCarthy is hopefully of that mindset. Trunnion : We waited for the 6th round to draft a defensive lineman. Is our defensive line set for starters and depth, and how are they…

title: Minkah Fitzpatrick reflects on frustration with Steelers
summary: Minkah Fitzpatrick was the missing ingredient to a defense that needed a splash playmaker. After Ben Roethlisberger went down with a season-ending elbow injury in Week 2 of the 2019 season, the Pittsburgh Steelers showed they weren’t mailing in the campaign and traded a first-round pick to the Miami Dolphins in exchange for the young […]
full_text: Minkah Fitzpatrick was the missing ingredient to a defense that needed a splash playmaker. After Ben Roethlisberger went down with a season-ending elbow injury in Week 2 of the 2019 season, the Pittsburgh Steelers showed they weren’t mailing in the campaign and traded a first-round pick to the Miami Dolphins in exchange for the young safety, and it ended up being one of the best trades in franchise history. From 2019-24, Fitzpatrick was a three-time First-Team All-Pro and a five-time Pro Bowler, leading the NFL in interceptions in 2022 with six. However, his splash plays began to decrease. From 2023-24, he recorded just one interception, and in June, 2025, he was sent back to the Dolphins in exchange for Jalen Ramsey and Jonnu Smith. Joining The Pivot, Fitzpatrick discussed the frustrations he had over the course of his final years with the Steelers. “When I first got there, they just kind of plugged me in at the post safety, half safety,” Fitzpatrick said . “And I played well there. After a while, quarterbacks aren’t going to be throwing you the ball a whole lot, or throwing [the post] or to your half. And I kind of got pushed into that role. And people forgot that what I was known for was my versatility and doing different things. I think I’m a good football player, so no matter where you put me on the field, I’m gonna be a good football player. But I think where my capabilities are maximized is when I can do different things. Whether it be in the post, next play in the half, next play rushing off the edge – doing different things. And I think they got so used to me being in that role, and doing a good job of it… I just got stuck in that role. And after a while, my splash and production went down. I was still playing ‘good football,’ but it wasn’t splashy football. And I just got stuck in a role that wasn’t splashy, wasn’t making a lot of plays…” Fitzpatrick’s soliloquy confirms what a lot of fans and media have been saying about the defense over the last handful of years. Schematically, they had grown stale and showed an inability to adapt and evolve. Through training camp, we’ve seen new defensive coordinator Patrick Graham experiment and try new things with his top players, specifically as it pertains to the edge rushers. Graham has thrown looks at the offense with T.J. Watt lined up all over the defensive line, as well as Alex Highsmith. We’ve also seen looks with Watt, Highsmith, and Nick Herbig all on the field at the same time. While we still have to see what it looks like in game, the early changes and nuances through the final weeks of summer have been refreshing, and something the Steelers have desperately needed. title: Elijah Arroyo’s rookie Seahawks tape wasn’t flashy, but provides reasons for optimism
summary: When the Seattle Seahawks selected Elijah Arroyo in the second round of the 2026 NFL Draft, John Schneider made it clear the organization believed it had landed far more talent than the draft slot suggested. The general manager even remarked that, had Arroyo remained healthy throughout college, he would have been viewed as one of […]
full_text: When the Seattle Seahawks selected Elijah Arroyo in the second round of the 2026 NFL Draft, John Schneider made it clear the organization believed it had landed far more talent than the draft slot suggested. The general manager even remarked that, had Arroyo remained healthy throughout college, he would have been viewed as one of the top players in the class—a statement that illustrated just how highly Seattle valued his upside. That kind of praise naturally raises expectations. While it’s easy to understand why the Seahawks were excited about his athletic profile, projecting any rookie as one of the best players in an entire draft class places an enormous burden on a player who had already battled injuries before entering the league. Seattle essentially viewed the draft as adding three premium talents: first-round pick Grey Zabel, early second-round selection Nick Emmanwori, and Arroyo, whose talent they believed exceeded where he was selected. The rookie season, however, never quite unfolded the way many envisioned. Rather than immediately becoming a featured weapon in Klint Kubiak’s offense, Arroyo spent much of the year trying to carve out a consistent role within Seattle’s tight end rotation. The flashes were evident, but the production rarely matched the potential. That doesn’t necessarily mean the process was disappointing. The tape still reveals a player with traits that are difficult to teach. What stood out on Elijah Arroyo’s tape A different type of tight end What immediately stands out watching Arroyo is that he doesn’t play like a traditional in-line tight end. Seattle drafted him because he brings a different skill set to the position. His size, movement skills and catch radius allow him to function almost as a hybrid receiver, creating difficult matchups against linebackers while also possessing enough size to challenge safeties over the middle of the field. Arroyo as the X forces the defense to declare coverage: a LB/S matching him suggests man, while a CB points toward zone. He also wins the catch point with strength and his frame—traits that could be especially valuable in Seattle's play-action game. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-11T01:19:16.513Z This is something worth watching repeatedly. Arroyo lining up as the X receiver forces the defense to declare its coverage. If a linebacker or a safety rotates down to match him, it’s a strong indicator of man coverage; if a cornerback stays responsible for him, it points more toward zone. On this rep, Arroyo also wins the physical battle at the catch point, using his frame and strength to create separation from the defender and come down with a tough reception. That combination of alignment versatility and physicality could make him particularly valuable for Seattle’s offense. Those traits become particularly valuable in play-action concepts, where linebackers are forced to step toward the line of scrimmage before recovering into coverage. Vertical stress creates opportunities Although he isn’t an elite route runner yet, Arroyo has enough speed to threaten the seam. That vertical element forces defenses to account for him differently than they would many traditional tight ends. His presence has value beyond his own statistics. Arroyo's seam ability can stretch coverage between the hashes, opening space underneath for Jaxon Smith-Njigba while complementing Seattle's run and play-action game. It's the role he seemed best suited for as a rookie, even if Seattle never fully unlocked it — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-11T01:21:25.342Z A seam-running tight end stretches coverage between the hashes, creating additional room for players like Jaxon Smith-Njigba underneath while also complementing Seattle’s running game and play-action concepts. That’s the role Arroyo appeared best suited to fill entering his rookie season, even if the offense never fully unlocked it. Play-action should remain central to Seattle's offense. The school […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 26: Chris Carson #32 of the Seattle Seahawks runs the ball for a touchdown during the second quarter in the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 26, 2021 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images A former Seattle Seahawk is sticking around the area — and the game. A little over four years after running back Chris Carson announced his retirement due to a neck injury suffered during the 2021 season, he has joined the staff of Redmond High School’s football team, the Mustangs, as running backs coach. The school announced the high-profile addition to their staff on Instagram (with a hat tip to Field Gulls reader Bubba for posting this in The Feed ). View this post on Instagram Despite entering the league as a seventh-round pick, following the 2017 NFL Draft, Carson immediately brought excitement into what was then a middling running back room. By Week 2 of his rookie season, Carson had taken the reigns in a 20-carry, 93-yard showing against the 49ers, but his season ended after four games due to a broken ankle. Carson rebounded as a sophomore, putting together the first in what was back-to-back 1,000-yard campaigns. Across 49 career games with Seattle, Carson rushed for 3,502 yards and 24 touchdowns, with another 804 yards and seven scores through the air. Now, as a member of Redmond’s coaching staff, Carson joins a long line of Pete Carroll-era Seahawks to stick around the area in retirement.

summary: We get to watch the San Francisco 49ers play football. Maybe not the starters, but there will be enough battles that play out during preseason that’ll be worth the watch. full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 14: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers shakes hands with Cam Ward #1 of the Tennessee Titans after the game at Levi's Stadium on December 14, 2025 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images We get to watch the San Francisco 49ers play football. Maybe not the starters, but there will be enough battles that play out during preseason that’ll be worth the watch. Who are you looking forward to watching? Who should play extended snaps? Onto today’s links. Top five things to watch for in the 49ers’ preseason opener vs. Titans (paywall) “The decision between a third stack linebacker, a fifth defensive back at nickel or a fifth on-the-ball lineman seemed to lead Morris to that newly named fever backer position. The idea is to have a player capable of handling the responsibilities for three different positions, all in one. Nick Martin and Jaden Dugger, a raw rookie who played safety, linebacker and stand-up edge in college, have gotten familiar with the role. Morris has even thrown Romello Height, a dynamic rookie speed rusher, into the fever backer conversation. It would make sense for all three, none of whom are established starters, to play Thursday. The position boils down to the 11th man providing versatility, which makes things more difficult for an offense trying to read the defense before the snap. “Obviously, you know what traditional backers look like,” Morris said. “Stand-up guys that can move around. Those fever backers are kind of those guys that bring you subtle changes, subtle different things. … They can play star (nickel) for you. They can play outside edge and play sort of a big nickel. They can get at the line of scrimmage.” Morris was asked whether fever backer is a staple or more situational in his defense; he said it depends. The preseason may offer a sense of how much.” 49ers’ Brock Purdy carved up the Titans, but offensive line concerns are growing (paywall) “Niners defensive coordinator Raheem Morris came up with the nickname early in training camp when talking about the quarterback’s touch, though Purdy is not the biggest fan of it. Why? “Our quarterbacks coach, Mick Lombardi, doesn’t like the word ‘layer.’ He thinks everything should be driven,” Purdy said with a smile. “It’s cool that Raheem notices that, so I guess it’s a part of my game. But obviously, I like to think I can make any throw in the field, not just that one.” 49ers roster moves: RB Zamir White among 3 signed; 3 players waived “Throughout his four-year NFL career with the Raiders (2022-25), Zamir White has appeared in 45 games (nine starts) and registered 198 carries for 736 yards and two touchdowns on the ground, along with 25 receptions for 152 yards through the air. In 2025, White appeared in six games and totaled 12 carries for 32 yards and added four receptions for 24 yards.” What 49ers rookie Kaelon Black has learned watching Christian McCaffrey practice “The way that he runs his routes, how efficient he is,” Black said. “When I watch him at practice, he has no wasted movement. “I asked him, ‘What do you do to limit your wasted movement?’ And he said, ’It’s all about timing and just being yourself.’” Rookie Kaelon Black outlines why 49ers’ offensive system is perfect fit for him “It really maximizes what a running back can truly do. A lot of times running backs aren’t asked to catch the ball a lot out of the backfield. But here, it’s the complete opposite. You’re going to go out there and run different routes and you’re almost going to feel like a receiver first sometimes.” Kawakami: Brock Purdy and the 3 WRs who are saving the first part of 49ers camp (paywall) “I didn’t think it was feasible that Deebo could run the ball more than once or twice a game; I thought his wide back days were over. And yet … Deebo has lined up at RB at times from the moment he returned to the 49ers and he was by far their most dangerous RB on Tuesday. He also caught a couple of passes as a WR and generally was a major problem for the Titans throughout.” 49ers add a running back ahead of the preseason opener; waive Junior Bergen “Bergen might be a surprise, as some reporters who were present at practice went so far as to say he could sneak onto the roster and was viewed as the top option at punt returner. The team felt differently. They could bring Bergen back if he clears waivers, but the 49ers being comfortable with losing him on waivers with a slew of injuries at the position tells us how they feel about him.”

Because of that, the team had three running backs in the building on Monday. One was on a visit, with two others for tryouts. Despite hosting Watson for a visit, the team signed former Raiders running back Zamir White. That wasn’t the only transaction the team made. They also signed cornerback Eli Apple and defensive lineman Xavier Thomas, along with White, all to one-year deals. The Niners were unlikely to use Deebo Samuel in the backfield in a preseason game the same way they did during their joint practice. That leaves Khalil Herbert, Patrick Taylor, and Sincere McCormick as the three healthy bodies in the backfield. Shoot, even Kyle Juszczyk is dealing with an injury . Another back was needed. White was a fourth-round pick of the Raiders in 2022. His most productive season was in 2023, when White ran for 451 yards and had 98 receiving yards. White, 26, only had 12 carries for Las Vegas last year. He’s 6’, 215 pounds. The corresponding moves were to waive wide receiver Junior Bergen, punter Jack Bouwmeester, and to waive/injured edge rusher K.J. Henry. So, at least for now, the punting competition is over. Bergen might be a surprise, as some reporters who were present at practice went so far as to say he could sneak onto the roster and was viewed as the top option at punt returner. The team felt differently. They could bring Bergen back if he clears waivers, but the 49ers being comfortable with losing him on waivers with a slew of injuries at the position tells us how they feel about him.

title: 3 questions for the 49ers at WR: Can this group stay healthy?
summary: No position has been more volatile over the past couple of years for the San Francisco 49ers than wide receiver. Oddly enough, from 2019-2024, the position was maybe the sturdiest of all position groups, with some variation of Deebo Samuel, Brandon Aiyuk, and Jauan Jennings leading. But now, just two years removed from that, the […]
full_text: No position has been more volatile over the past couple of years for the San Francisco 49ers than wide receiver. Oddly enough, from 2019-2024, the position was maybe the sturdiest of all position groups, with some variation of Deebo Samuel, Brandon Aiyuk, and Jauan Jennings leading. But now, just two years removed from that, the 49ers have a completely new receiving corps, with only Samuel left, but after a quick departure for a cup of coffee (one bound to make Aiyuk jealous) with Washington. With so much change at the position over the last two seasons, there’s bound to be plenty of questions. Let’s ask just three of those questions today: Can the position group stay healthy? What the 49ers offense was able to do in 2025 with the multiple fires at receiver it had to put out is nothing short of remarkable. It started with what seemed to be a normal recovery window for Brandon Aiyuk after his 2024 knee injury, which then devolved into the star receiver going AWOL in a situation still not yet resolved. Ricky Pearsall was supposed to take his next step and showed that promise when he was on the field, but a knee injury held him to just nine games, and the lingering effects of the injury have cost Pearsall the 2026 season. Jauan Jennings was solid throughout the season, but the receiving corps struggled with Kendrick Bourne and DeMarcus Robinson playing key roles in the absences of Aiyuk and Pearsall. Not-a-wide-receiver Christian McCaffrey is who kept the position afloat, with his first 100-catch season since 2019. Wholesale changes came over the offseason with the 49ers signing veterans Mike Evans and Christian Kirk, while using the team’s first draft selection on De’Zhaun Stribling to shore up the unit. But Evans isn’t getting any younger and has dealt with some nagging injuries the last few seasons, while Kirk missed nine games just two years ago with a broken collarbone, and a calf injury has kept him out of training camp the past few weeks. On paper, the 49ers receiving corps is much better compared to what it was last year, but the moves made over the offseason didn’t exactly fend off the concerns of high-injury potential at the position. What can be expected from Deebo Samuel? With the news of Pearsall being out for the season, the 49ers wasted no time in setting up the reunion with Deebo Samuel. While it’s fun to rekindle the memories of what Samuel meant to the 49ers in his first stint, it would be downright insane to think that that version of Deebo Samuel could make an appearance in 2026. While the role of an all-use offensive weapon might be reprised, it will be on a far lesser scale for a now 30-year-old Samuel. Samuel was brought in as the replacement for Pearsall, but his role will be vastly different; I think he was brought in more as a reprieve for the injuries in the running back group than for the receiving corps. The best-case scenario for Samuel is being the No. 3 receiver on the team, behind Evans and Stribling, while there’s even a chance somebody like Kirk or Robinson could out-target him. But the role is already laid out: he’s likely to step into some spots where McCaffrey would have been used last season out of necessity. Because of Deebo, instead of forcing a top-three running back in the league to it, you can use a player like Samuel to take some of the unnecessary wear-and-tear McCaffrey took in 2025. He likely won’t be near the 90-touch plateau he’s been at the last few seasons, but Samuel’s role will be an important one, especially if he can take some of the workload off of McCaffrey with roughly the same production. What is the first-year ceiling for De’Zhaun Stribling? There has been no player on the 49ers whose stock has grown over the first few weeks of training camp like Stribling. Part of that growth has come from Stribling himself, while some factors around him certainly haven’t hurt his cause. When the 49ers made Stribling the 33rd selection in last April’s draft, the pick certainly turned some heads. Not even factoring that Stribling wasn’t considered a top receiver in the draft at the time, the pick was head-scratching with the then-recent signings of Evans and Kirk, with Pearsall expected to be ready to play. In essence, the 49ers used their top pick on a player who would enter camp as the team’s No. 4 receiver. As things tend to do in the NFL, the situation changed. Kirk has dealt with an injury that has kept him out of camp, and Pearsall has been lost for the 2026 season. Those injuries alone have launched Stribling into the conversation to be the 49ers’ No. 2 receiver entering the regular season. Players typically don’t earn spots due to injury in the NFL, but Stribling’s play during training camp has done the most to earn him the consideration for the spot behind Evans. It’s tough to go a day reading training camp reports without some sort of mention of Stribling’s performance. While we have seen players, specifically receivers (think Trent Sherfield), jump off the page with solid training camp performances, it’s hard to not be excited for what Stribling can be with how much he has meshed with the 49ers since drafted.

title: K.J. Wright on 49ers rookie: ‘He is that guy I saw on film”
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have been preaching versatility on defense under new defensive coordinator Raheem Morris, and perhaps no player has symbolized that more than fifth-round rookie linebacker Jaden Dugger. Dugger, a safety-converted-MIKE in college, fits what the 49ers have generally liked with their linebackers from an athleticism perspective. But there’s a lot more to […]
full_text: LAFAYETTE, LA - SEPTEMBER 27: Jaden Dugger #3 of the Ragin' Cajuns celebrates making a tackle during the first overtime Louisiana v Marshall Football at Our Lady of Lourdes Stadium at Cajun Field on September 27, 2025 in Lafayette, Louisiana. (Photo by Ragin' Cajuns Athletics/university Images via Getty images) The San Francisco 49ers have been preaching versatility on defense under new defensive coordinator Raheem Morris, and perhaps no player has symbolized that more than fifth-round rookie linebacker Jaden Dugger. Dugger, a safety-converted-MIKE in college, fits what the 49ers have generally liked with their linebackers from an athleticism perspective. But there’s a lot more to the puzzle, as the 49ers have moved him around all three linebacker spots and even played him in some other roles off the edge, despite it being his first offseason with the team. “Every day of practice, [he] plays the MIKE, WILL, and the star position,” linebackers coach K.J. Wright said of Dugger. “And now throw him a curveball, he’s gonna play D-line. You’re like, what? That can do a lot to a player’s mind. I kid you not, guys, he handled it pitch perfect. He went with the D-line, he rushed, he set the edge, showed some really good versatility. He did one-on-ones against the running backs, made it look easy. “And so he is a linebacker. Like he’s not a D-lineman, he is a linebacker. But as time goes on, things happen. We need a 3rd down package. Hey, you go play defensive end, you go burn that edge and go get after that quarterback. He can do that. But his main position is a linebacker, but he can also down the line showcase that he can go on the line of scrimmage, be extra valuable for us.” And this versatility isn’t new. Wright identified it on tape when scouting Dugger and felt more confident in the rookie after interviewing him during the pre-draft scouting process. “I knew [he could be versatile] when I interviewed him in April or whatever. I knew, I was like, this guy can handle multiple [positions]. He did it in college,” Wright said. “A guy that played safety, a guy that played on the ball, a guy that went to MIKE linebacker. I knew that he could handle what we’re asking him to do. It’s not easy, but for a guy to be able to play 3 positions, guys, 3 positions in practice is really cool to see. I’m just excited for his future. We meet every day as rookies, each and every practice. We get on the board, tell me what you see. I hand him the clicker, you’re the coach, and we just talk it out.” Dugger is still relatively new to the linebacker position after starting his college career as a safety. And the 49ers understand that, and are looking to continue developing him at the position. But there were clear positives on tape that Wright identified which made him confident that Dugger could be a fit in San Francisco. “I’m going to ask questions. I’m going to ask football questions. I’m going to get on the tape. Tell me what you see,” Wright continued about his pre-draft meeting with Dugger. “Walk me through your progression throughout the week and how you get ready to play a football game. I can tell guys who have a plan. I can tell guys who don’t have a plan. And he was a guy that had a plan. He had a regimen. He had a routine. And for him to just play Mike at Louisiana Lafayette, his just one year, I knew that he was still raw. He still had some growing and developing to do. He’s still growing. It’s, what, practice 10? Yeah, he’s going to keep getting better each and every time he steps on the football field.” Now, through nearly a full offseason, Wright is seeing the film play out on the field with Dugger’s athleticism, and he feels the rookie is going to be a player. “And the thing is with Dugger, like, he is that guy that I saw on film,” Wright added. “You guys see this man run from the numbers to the other numbers, like he covers so much grass, you know what I mean? When you see him tackle, like, we don’t obviously tackle, we see him like make contact, he’s the guy that can sink into his hips. Same way that he was in college. “It’s just my job to make sure that keep tapping to those to those strengths that he has, but also let’s keep developing, taking on linemen. Let’s keep developing striking, get comfortable in front of the huddle because you know it’s about to be about sixty thousand fans out there next week. You got to be loud. You got to be vocal. You got to get everybody on the same page and so on. It’s obviously growing pains as a rookie, but as time goes on, he’s going to be a guy.”

title: Commanders fans are getting the Jake Moody experience familiar to 49ers fans
summary: Washington Commanders fans are getting the Jake Moody experience San Francisco 49ers fans know so well. The former 49ers kicker is competing for the Commanders’ placekicker job, a situation not unlike the one he was in just one year ago. The difference is, the 49ers released Gregg Joseph, Moody’s competitor, because Moody won the competition […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 30: Jake Moody #16 of the Washington Commanders looks on prior to an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Northwest Stadium on November 30, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Washington Commanders fans are getting the Jake Moody experience San Francisco 49ers fans know so well. The former 49ers kicker is competing for the Commanders’ placekicker job, a situation not unlike the one he was in just one year ago. The difference is, the 49ers released Gregg Joseph, Moody’s competitor, because Moody won the competition early in training camp. In Washington, it’s the other way around for Moody, who is pitted against Drew Stevens. Per Grant Paulsen, Moody has missed 11 kicks in the last four practices. His misses on Monday? Jake Moody just went 2 for 6 in this kicking period. Four straight misses from 44, 49, 51, 55. He’s missed 11 kicks in the last 4 practices. — Grant Paulsen (@GrantPaulsen) August 10, 2026 On paper, Joseph was beating Moody at the time of the former’s release on August 4 by a single made kick. It was speculated that kickoff placement and confidence were the reasons to hold onto Moody, who was the 49ers’ first pick in the 2023 NFL Draft—a third-round pick, mind you, because they didn’t have a first or second that year. Moody was waived after Week 1 in the NFL regular season, two days after going 1 for 3 against the Seattle Seahawks . It almost looked like one that got away. When Moody left the 49ers, he went to the Chicago Bears practice squad and was called up in Week 6 when the Bears played the Commanders. Moody set a franchise record for most successful field goal attempts in a debut, going 4-5. He made all four of his kicks the following week against the New Orleans Saints. Unfortunately, Moody was only a placeholder while starter Cairo Santos dealt with injury. He went back to the practice squad and was signed by the Commanders to their active roster in November. Now he’s in another competition to get a starting job. He’s had a couple of good games, but it’s buried in bad practices and some head-scratching misses. Consistency might be what defines Jake Moody’s career. While the third-round pick used on him can be lambasted, it’s hard to imagine that he’d struggle this much three years later.

title: 49ers News: Sounds like the joint practice was LIT
summary: Fred Warner de-escalates fiery, fight-filled 49ers-Titans joint practice“The 49ers had two notable plays on back-to-back snaps highlighted by plays from defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa and safety Ji’Ayir Brown. Odighizuwa supplied pressure up the middle and grabbed a handful of Titans quarterback Cam Ward’s jersey as he ran past. The Titans did not take kindly to […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 04: Fred Warner #54 of the San Francisco 49ers juggles softballs while working out during training camp at SAP Performance Facility on August 04, 2023 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fred Warner de-escalates fiery, fight-filled 49ers-Titans joint practice “ The 49ers had two notable plays on back-to-back snaps highlighted by plays from defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa and safety Ji’Ayir Brown. Odighizuwa supplied pressure up the middle and grabbed a handful of Titans quarterback Cam Ward’s jersey as he ran past. The Titans did not take kindly to Odighizuwa touching their quarterback during the joint practice. On the next play, Brown sniffed out a Ward throw over the deep middle for an interception. The Titans were unable to connect down the field against the 49ers’ defensive backfield.” Fred Warner drops eye-popping praise about ‘sticky’ 49ers defensive backs “The way they’re playing, sticky in coverage, playing the ball in the air, being able to play the run game or the ball thrown the flat, the ability to tackle, I think it’s one of the best I’ve seen thus far,” Warner said. “I’m really excited about what I’m seeing. We just got to continue to jell and mesh that thing together so it’s the best version for when that time comes.” Fred Warner, 49ers’ pass defense stand out in heated session with Titans’ Cam Ward (paywall) “ But the bulk of Ward’s completions came on screens and short throws, and his best opportunities deep down the field couldn’t be hauled in by his receivers. He was twice flushed from the pocket by third-round rookie Romello Height. On another play, Ward forced a throw to Wan’Dale Robinson in tight coverage, allowing safety Ji’Ayir Brown to step forward and pick off the pass. That play also ended in a brief dustup involving cornerbacks Green and Upton Stout. During the ensuing delay, Warner walked from the sideline to the east end zone, raising both arms to pump up the crowd. After all, it’s been a while since he’s been able to do that. “That’s why I love joint practices,” he said afterward. “You really have an opportunity to work on your craft and really see where your team is….I don’t know if I’ve felt that confident in that part of the game as I feel right now,” he said. “That’s not a knock on any team that I’ve played with before. But I think this group is kind of meshing together, playing together, sticky in coverage, playing the ball in the air. … I think it’s one of the best I’ve seen thus far. I’m really excited.” 2026 San Francisco 49ers training camp: Latest intel, updates “I had Purdy at 21-of-27 on the day, including multiple touchdown passes and no interceptions. His best throws came in a move the ball sequence in which he dropped a perfect ball between three defenders to rookie WR De’Zhaun Stribling that would have gone for a long touchdown. And then, he had another layered throw over linebacker Cody Barton for a big gain to TE Jake Tonges.” 49ers’ Nick Bosa has knee tendinitis after ACL recovery, per Kyle Shanahan “Just soreness, tendinitis,” Shanahan said. “It’s a pretty normal thing with ACLs. Talking with our guys (medical staff), it happens with about 90 percent of the guys we’ve had.” How the 49ers’ defense looks different under Raheem Morris “The goal, not unlike coach Kyle Shanahan’s offense, is to utilize personnel groupings that make everything look the same before quickly transforming into something else. Through the first two weeks of camp, three young 49ers — second-year linebacker Nick Martin and rookies Jaden Dugger and Romello Height — have emerged as the top candidates for the job. Each has done one of those jobs well over their career, but they’re trying to add other tools to their belt throughout camp. It’s why Dugger spent some time at a recent practice with the defensive line, working to hone his pass-rush moves. And it’s why observers have seen Height take reps dropping into coverage. Martin has also occasionally lined up as the fifth defender on the line of scrimmage during team periods in this camp. Linebacker coach K.J. Wright said the winner of that competition, which he says is still wide open, won’t claim the job just based on physical attributes. They’ll have to prove they can handle the workload that accompanies so many responsibilities. Hence the position’s name.”

title: Commanders QB Jayden Daniels measured after excellent joint practice
summary: Head over to Twitter (I just can’t call it X) or Blue Sky or Threads, or whichever quick-twitch social platform you prefer. Type “Jayden Daniels” into the search field and scan the recent results.   Or simply scan the observations Scott Jennings collected in Hogs Haven’s “Sights and Sounds” post chronicling Washington’s joint practice with […]
full_text: Head over to Twitter (I just can’t call it X) or Blue Sky or Threads, or whichever quick-twitch social platform you prefer. Type “Jayden Daniels” into the search field and scan the recent results. Or simply scan the observations Scott Jennings collected in Hogs Haven’s “Sights and Sounds” post chronicling Washington’s joint practice with Miami. They all say the same thing. Daniels dominated the Dolphins with surgical accuracy, pushing the ball downfield or making smart, timely throws working through his progress. That’s hardly new for the third-year Commanders quarterback, who has been on one in recent training camp practices. It’s not just the Stefon Diggs addition or Terry McLaurin’s top-flight play. Daniels is working the same way with most receivers, putting the ball in just the right spot way more often than not. Daniels’ accuracy has always been there, but to see the precision at this point in the summer, while learning new coordinator David Blough’s system , has been super impressive. Daniels pumped the brakes on the hype train after Wednesday’s joint practice, saying there’s plenty of room for improvement despite early-camp success. “We’ve had some explosive plays and stuff like that, but a lot of it’s not perfect,” Daniels said in a post-practice press conference. “I’m still working. The whole team’s still working. We’re still building that chemistry and continuity. We’ve still got a long way to go.” That’s definitely true, but it doesn’t damped results like this mid-practice sequence. Then another one to Chig and another one to Terry. https://t.co/YghQYtjxmw — Nicki Jhabvala (@NickiJhabvala) August 12, 2026 Here’s video of that Daniels-Burks gem: Jayden Daniels —> Treylon Burks TD bomb pic.twitter.com/got2iddFZR — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) August 12, 2026 Practice tracking can be overblown, but this gives an idea of what Daniels was able to do against the Dolphins defense (which is admittedly subpar). From our friend @FullCommandShow: https://t.co/3A2QLaBdHK pic.twitter.com/QBMqxwumLG — Full Command (@FullCommandShow) August 12, 2026 All that shows there’s progress being made in terms of chemistry with his receivers and overall schematic mastery. That’s true even with extra requirements over a year ago, like huddling and operating largely under center while conducting all the pre-snap motions OC David Blough requires. “With reps, and as time goes on, you get more of a grasp for who can run what route, how Blough wants to call things – that’s what practice is for,” Daniels said. “Day-by-day, I try to have greater control of the offense and get 1% better.” Daniels was already pretty good. That was clear during his rookie year, and even at times during an injury-plagues 2025 campaign. While Commanders fans know that, it was also clear from the outside. “He’s one of the greatest playmakers in the league,” said Commanders linebacker Leo Chenal , who was in Kansas City the past four seasons. “We’ve all seen what he’s capable of. When I wasn’t here, I thought, ‘Dang, that dude’s a playmaker.’ You just see it. You have to respect that and what he’s able to do with the ball in his hand. “ Considering we might not see Daniels much this preseason – maybe a series or two? — this joint practice provides a solid progress report on the quarterback and the offense overall through a few weeks of camp. The joint practice in Baltimore on Aug. 26 will provide a better one as Daniels works to ramp up and get ready to hit the ground running this season. While Daniels isn’t one to pat himself on the back, he pinpointed areas where the Commanders offense has made strides. “Our play style. The intentionality that we have, that Blough wants for our system,” Daniels said. “Guys are stepping up and being leaders within the huddle. If we’re not meeting the standard of breaking the huddle and lining up with some urgency, somebody else will say it if I’m not saying anything. As the days progress, just the intensity, the intentionality of the concepts needs to grow. We’ll make mistakes in practice, but we’ll keep working at them.” He has made strides and some really nice plays thus far, but development must continue as we head for September. “I’m just trying to be the best version of myself,” Daniels said, “every day.”

summary: The Washington Commanders training camp rolls on for Day 11 in Ashburn, VA. full_text: The Washington Commanders training camp rolls on for Day 11 in Ashburn, VA. Today will be a little different, with the Miami Dolphins in town for a joint practice Wednesday morning and the first preseason game on Friday night. Head coach Dan Quinn spoke to reporters before the start of Wednesday’s practice. Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels and linebacker Leo Chenal also held Q&As after practice, while other players were interviewed on the field. Quinn outlined the structure of the joint practice, which would entail relatively short periods with an emphasis on 1-on-1s, red-zone work, 7-on-7s, team drills, including drive-the-ball work, two-minute drills and you-call-it segments. He didn’t provide much information on who would play in Friday’s preseason contest against the Dolphins, preferring to hold that information until game day. It’s safe to say, though, that first-team guys who work a ton in the joint practices probably won’t play in the game. Daniels had an excellent practice by all accounts, showing the pinpoint accuracy that has become commonplace during this training camp. title: Commanders News: McLaurin, all smiles after ‘hardest year’ of his life
summary: The Daily Slop – 12 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles The Athletic (paywall) […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 15: Terry McLaurin #17 of the Washington Commanders warms up before the game against the New York Giants at Northwest Stadium on September 15, 2024 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by G Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 12 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles The Athletic (paywall) Commanders’ Terry McLaurin feels free after enduring ‘hardest year’ of his life “This last year was the hardest year of my life — from the contract and getting hurt, and you know, I’ve been going through some stuff off the field, just personally,” McLaurin revealed Friday. “It’s been extremely challenging.” “I’ve been somebody who’s kind of struggled with worry, struggled with anxiety, sometimes not feeling good enough. So when you go through contract stuff, when you go through injury, it can kind of make you feel insecure at times.” “From the contract and getting hurt, I’ve been going through some stuff off the field, just personally; it’s been extremely challenging.” Terry McLaurin “[Now], I just feel like I’m in a great space. … I wouldn’t trade anything because it’s built me into the person I am right now, and I just feel like I’m playing with a type of freedom that I haven’t had. So I’m just looking forward to spilling that out for my team this year.” Two owners, four head coaches, four offensive coordinators, four wide receivers coaches, an astounding 15 starting quarterbacks, and yet, McLaurin always delivered. He recorded five straight 1,000-yard seasons from 2020 to 2024, and during his second Pro Bowl season (2024), racked up a career-high 13 touchdown catches. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN Brandon Coleman says he wishes he had trained like this in the past Coleman missed time in his rookie training camp because of a shoulder injury. From Weeks 9 to 17 as a rookie, he played every snap but missed 18 in the regular-season finale. “There’s injuries that I’ve had in the past during training camp,” Coleman said, “that fully could have been prevented if I would’ve just sacrificed a little more time in rehab and working on certain things.” To help, Coleman said he has taken more care to use preventative maintenance on his body — from how he stretches to how he eats, to his daily recovery sessions after workouts. He hired a nutritionist. He worked out with Dominic Studzinski, a former Ole Miss strength and conditioning coach who has trained Tunsil for more than a decade. “Just taking care of myself a lot better,” Coleman said. “There are priorities I didn’t do the first couple years that I just have to reflect on and kind of be accountable on. I changed that last year, but then even more this year.” That included spending several weeks training with Tunsil in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, this summer. “I dragged my wife out there to the middle of nowhere,” Coleman said. “What she understood is just really seeing how one of the greatest tackles ever does it. How do I need to live to give myself a chance to be like that guy?” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated The Good and Not So Good From Commanders’ Tenth Training Camp Practice Several veterans received maintenance days, which shifted reps to younger players and roster-battle candidates ahead of Wednesday’s joint session with Miami. On the day: Joshua Josephs continued forcing his way into the conversation, Antonio Williams produced multiple touchdowns, and Washington’s backup tight ends made several plays. Josephs beat Brandon Coleman with a rip move quickly enough that the play might have been a sack in live football. Later in the day, Josephs was able to disrupt things again with another would-be sack, this time on Marcus Mariota. It will be interesting to watch Josephs line up against the Dolphins tackles Wednesday to get a good sense of what we are working with there. His quickness and motor are impressive. Cager grabbed two touchdowns from Mariota, including a seam route on the first play of the two-minute period that left him open for an uncontested score. Yankoff continued to receive a healthy number of targets and added to a camp in which his athleticism and receiving ability have consistently stood out. The two have been forcing the Commanders to decide whether they want a fourth tight end and then who it should be, all at the same time. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Riggo’s Rag Javon Kinlaw set to be unleashed in new-look Commanders defense Kinlaw’s already loving how the plan is unfolding at training camp. He explained the variety to reporters after a recent practice . “I’m getting to play everywhere. The shade, the two wide, the three, the four, the five, the six. I’m playing it all, man. I’m loving how I’m getting to just give guys different looks and be all over the place, man. And I think it’s going to play to my strengths well, man. You know, give a lot of guys fits.” This is an intriguing, multi-faceted role for Kinlaw. One that only shows how much the Commanders still believe in his so far largely untapped talents. The new approach to deploying big No. 99 is also the latest example of how first-year play-caller Jones is willing to find creative ways to get underperforming senior personnel more involved . This isn’t the first time the Commanders have planned to move Kinlaw from the interior to the edge. Jones’ predecessor, Joe Whitt Jr., wanted to do the same , but there’s a little extra nuance to this year’s attempts to unleash the South Carolina product. First, the system Jones is likely to call, the type he learned from Brian Flores with the Minnesota Vikings, is more elaborate. He’ll use moving pieces to disguise coverage and pressure in ways Whitt rarely did. That’s good news for Kinlaw, who could find himself facing more one-on-one matchups against offensive linemen on the lookout for blitzing linebackers and defensive backs. Few individual blockers are going to want to stand up to the 6-foot-5, 319-pound player on the edge. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Officially Sign DT Byron Cowart Among Three Roster Moves https://t.co/P5uwVA36IH — NFLTradeRumors.co (@nfltrade_rumors) August 11, 2026 Commanders.com Joint practice with Dolphins believed to be first-ever on Ashburn grounds [N]o, this isn’t one of those cutesy “firsts” where there was a joint practice held here when the facility had a different name. The records show (and team personnel close to the matter say) that tomorrow will be the first time an official NFL joint practice will be held on the Ashburn grounds. A lot of logistics need to be hammered out to successfully host a joint practice for an NFL organization – everything from perhaps the more straightforward hotel accommodation details to how a team will move to and from the practice fields to temporary on-site work spaces for traveling support staff. Most facilities weren’t designed to host two full NFL teams, so communication and planning are key. Visiting teams take site visits to the hosting organization’s facility months in advance, and regular meetings are held to discuss each team’s role (i.e. equipment, football video, athletic training) and how everything should be executed. All of this means teams are likely to host just one joint practice per preseason. The #Commanders welcome the #Dolphins to Ashburn.
